utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. We have today a tight schedule, and therefore I would propose the following schedule, so as to enable for Defence counsel to make their closing arguments: I propose that we be here in court from 9.00 to 10.30, when we'll take a 20-minute break; we'll resume at 10.50 until 12.20, so a second Defence counsel, and then we'll take a 10-minute break; we'll resume at 12.30 until 2.00. This would, as I say, enable three Defence counsel to speak each for an hour and a half, as agreed. Let us start right away. I assume Counsel Radovic will be the first one. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to apologise for the fact that I'm not a very good speaker; at any rate, not as good as the Prosecutor is. So if I do not manage to present my positions as well as he did, I apologise in advance. In addition to that, I shall make every effort, in my closing argument, to speak about the actual state of affairs as regards the indictment and the situation itself. I'm not going to go into partial accuracies or inaccuracies, as we've noted in the Prosecutor's closing argument. The most telling proof of this is that part of the closing argument of the Prosecutor where he says, in connection with the agreement reached on the 21st of October, 1992, that it was impossible to hear anyone with regard to that agreement except for the accused Zoran Kupreskic himself, because there are no living witnesses who attended the signing of that agreement, that is quite inaccurate, and that is demonstrated by the fact that in the last list of witnesses that was presented by the Prosecutor was the name of Fuad Berbic. Fuad Berbic was a participant in this agreement. So if anyone wanted to hear him on this subject as to how the talks and negotiations evolved, then Fuad Berbic was supposed to have been heard, not give up on his testimony altogether and then state in one's closing argument that there are no living persons who attended this agreement except for Zoran Kupreskic. The proceedings started by the issuing of the first indictment, dated the 2nd of November, 1995, which was confirmed, and in this indictment, the period involving the counts was from the 16th to the 25th of April, 1993. This indictment included Marinko Katava as well, who gave an interview to the Prosecutor and who raised the question of his alibi. Witness CD had already confirmed his alibi in another case, that is to say, in the case against Tihofil Blaskic. After the alibi of Marinko Katava was confirmed, the Prosecutor gave up on this because of his alibi for the 16th of April, 1993, and as for the other accused, in order to avoid that kind of a situation again, to have other accused prove where they were and what they did on the 16th of April, then the time scope was extended; that is to say, it started with October 1992 and it goes on until the end of April, as mentioned in the amended indictment. The indictment itself, as it stands now, makes Defence counsel face major difficulties, and these difficulties lie in the following: Yesterday, until the very end, when the Prosecutor responded to the question put by the President of the Trial Chamber as to whether the murder of Sukrija was being included or not, we did not know what this was all about. Did it relate only to the general part about persecution, or did it only involve the events in the house of protected Witness KO? That is why we objected on previous occasions as well, the indictment as it stands, and it is on its basis that the trial, as it evolved, does not have a factual basis. We are also invoking the case of Dusko Tadic, where the facts were specified, and it was well known what he was being indicted for. Also, we invoke the Furundzija case, where, at first, the indictment was ambiguous, so to speak, and then at the request of the Defence counsel, the Prosecutor had to say specifically what Furundzija was being indicted for, and then this was accepted, and finally, the indictment that was made showed exactly what was being sought. Now, one of the things that the accused are being indicted for is the planning, organisation, and execution of attacks; however, it is our claim that such actions can be carried out only by persons who have a certain political influence or the ability to command, the power to command. Zoran Kupreskic never belonged to such a circle of persons who would have any political or military power. It is interesting that the Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague had two persons who had great political power too, but they gave up on the Prosecution of these persons; that is, IT-95-14/2-PT, and another one, that is to say, Santic and Skopljak. First of all, we think that this trial contained less legal arguments. First and foremost, the factual situation has to be ascertained, and that is why we laid emphasis on that, that is to say, the establishment of facts. The indictment starts with the period beginning with October 1992, and there's no mention of any specific event that might have occurred. Why was this month selected to denote the beginning? During the proceedings, we lost a lot of time as we debated the conflict on the Vitez-Kiseljak road, by the Catholic cemetery, because the Prosecutor tried to portray this conflict to the Court as if it had been caused by the Croats; however, in his closing argument, the Prosecutor simply skips this conflict, and we do not believe that he has skipped it because he believes that everything is clear and everything has been proven and corroborated by evidence, or that he doesn't think that this conflict occurred at all on the 20th of October, but he skips over it because this conflict precisely shows that in Ahmici, there was an organised unit of the Muslim army which, at orders received from a higher command, had this road cut off. In order to prove that this is so, we have invoked a number of witnesses, primarily Prosecution witnesses, because we believe that Prosecution witnesses do not work in the interest of the Defence to help the accused, as it were. They are trying to help the other side, that is to say, the Prosecutor. So I wish to invoke the statement made by Witness Abdulah Ahmic, who said that the orders to place the roadblock came from the command of the Territorial Defence. Mehmed Ahmic, Witness B, and Fahrudin Ahmic, and Witness N and Witness AA, all say that the Muslims from Ahmici, assisted by Muslims from the village of Vrhovine, had the road cut off; that is to say that it is their military unit from Ahmici that did this and they received orders to that effect. As opposed to the Muslims from Ahmici, it has been undeniably proven that on this conflict on the 20th of October, 1992, not a single Croat from Ahmici participated in this. So we do not view this event any more as the event from which the incriminated period began, according to the indictment or the period of conflict, because although the Prosecutor mentions this in his brief, however we take that event as a circumstance which proves the contrary to what the Prosecutor is claiming. That is to say that in Ahmici indeed there was an organised armed unit of the Muslim forces. This will be mentioned later when we talk about whether there was an organised unit or whether these were simply armed civilians who were defending their homes, as the Prosecutor is trying to portray to the Court. He is also trying to say that the Muslim population was entitled to safeguard their homes with rifles in their hands, and that was considered to be normal, and that did not jeopardise their neighbours, whereas the three Croats in Grabovi, in the middle part of Ahmici, by virtue of the fact that they carried guns while they were on night guard, they jeopardised the Muslim population, and there were many more of them several times over. But then we are going to go back to that later. The next point that I would like to refer to relates to the road between Vitez and Kiseljak; namely, whether this road was of strategic importance for the HVO or, more precisely, for the military component of the HVO. Several witnesses were also heard with regard to this count. Perhaps the most interesting are the statements made by the Prosecutor witnesses. So I would like to mention the statement made by Brian Watters, who confirms that this road was of a strategic importance. In addition to his opinion, he says that this is what he was told by the Muslim General Halilovic. Michael Sean Dooley and Witness B also confirmed the strategic importance. And Matthew Robert also does this indirectly, although he does not say it directly. However, he does speak about it indirectly in the part where he speaks about the fact that every army tries to break up the military grouping of the enemy side into several parts and then these fragmented units are destroyed separately. After all, this is a well-known fact, not only in infantry battles, but also in sea battles, and even Admiral Nelson did this during the Battle of Trafalgar when he conquered the French fleet. However, it's nicer to see it when it's done by ships and navies. It's far more elegant than when it's done by infantry on the ground. But this was a strategic road and it was, after all, confirmed by the Crown witness, so to speak, the Crown witness of the Prosecution, and we were quite satisfied with that person, and the expert witness, Asim Dzambasovic. We also invoke his statement on several occasions because essentially this expert witness proved what the Defence sought to prove throughout the trial. The next point would be proving that there were military reasons for placing Ahmici under HVO control. I should kindly like to ask that when I elaborate these military reasons, that you do not understand this as us saying that there have to be civilian casualties. We are not saying that. No. We accept the fact that there were crimes committed and that there were civilian victims; however, we do not accept that there were not any military reasons involved when the decision was made to go to war. And at what level and on which side this was decided, we don't want to debate that, because we were never in a position to reach decisions on war and peace. We were not warlords. We were small people in the village of Ahmici, or on the outskirts of the village of Ahmici, bordering the Muslim part of the village of Ahmici. So as for civilian victims, we recognise what the Prosecutor said, although we say that we could not have known about this, nor did we participate in this. As for the assessment of what happened in Ahmici, I must say that I found the statement by Brian Watters strange. He claimed that Ahmici was attacked because Ahmici had a special religious importance for the Muslims, because several Imans come from Ahmici, more than usual than other Muslim communities. However, when we heard the testimonies of Muslims, including Witness EE and Abdulah Ahmic, none of them confirmed that fact. Therefore, if no one from Ahmici knows of this, that is to say that Ahmici would have a special emotional importance for Muslims from the Lasva River Valley area, then I believe that this special significance did not exist at all. It is the people of Ahmici who would have known about this better than anyone who could have whispered this into the ear of Witness Brian Watters. So this kind of information we can leave in the sphere of propaganda rather than proven facts, established facts. In P-1, -2 and -3, those exhibits, it is obvious that the road Vitez-Kiseljak passes through the lower part of the village of Ahmici and that on one side and the other side of that road there are houses. There are houses of Muslims, not only of Croats. In addition to that, the upper and the middle part of the village of Ahmici is above that road. Now, I have to draw your attention to the following: that is to say, the control over a road is not only achieved by physically taking the road. In military terminology there is an expression, "holding under fire control," which means that a side that has mortars, cannons, or any other kind of gunfire, and that can stop passage along that road by such means, can actually cut off the road and keep the road under its control in that way. The positions in Ahmici are such that if a side does not actually have control of the road physically, can through its gunfire from those positions exercise control over that road. The Prosecutor said that there were no Muslim soldiers in Ahmici and that these were armed civilians who, with a rifle in their hands, defended their homes. This thesis has legal impact; that is to say that these are civilians, persons, or groups of persons who are defending their homes. However, when an army is organised according to territorial principle, all soldiers are in their homes, soldiers who do not defend only their homes, but who, when they receive orders, can also launch an attack, just as the unit from Ahmici on the 20th of October, 1992 went to cut off the road, which was a crucial artery for the HVO. The Prosecutor evolved the following thesis: That is to say that in Ahmici there were no Muslim soldiers. He bases this on statements made by the British officers from the British Battalion; that is to say, Brian Watters, who claims that they never saw members of the Muslim army; that in Ahmici, when they saw persons who were killed, that there were no persons in military uniforms; and that in Ahmici there were no military facilities. However, this witness also allowed for the possibilities that among the dead there were bodies of soldiers not in uniform. Michael Sean Dooley and Matthew Robert said something similar, and so did Stephen Hughes. However, Stephen Hughes did see two corpses wearing parts of uniforms. However, it is not this part of their testimony that is important to us, because it refers to the military experience of a person serving in an army which has a tradition going back for several centuries, and where it is unimaginable that military personnel could go to war in civilian clothes, and that they might reside in buildings or camps and so on. Apart from this, we think that the testimony of the officer of the British Battalion is partly motivated by the terrible picture of the burnt-out village of Ahmici, all those gutted houses, which really looked dreadful, and the number of corpses, corpses not in uniform and without any insignia, military insignia. However, as regards uniforms, a better picture is provided by the members of the Muslim people from the village of Ahmici. The fact that there were no persons in uniform among those who were killed, or the fact that some of them had parts of uniforms, does not indicate that there were no soldiers there, because some soldiers did not have uniforms, while others had them at home but were not wearing them. Also, the fact that there were no military facilities in the village of Ahmici means absolutely nothing under conditions of Territorial Defence, especially in a village where there are many barns and similar places which can be used as arms and ammunition depots. So the whole village in fact is a military facility, and this is a basic fact of Territorial Defence which was not understood by the officers of the British Battalion. In spite of all our efforts to explain this, the Prosecutor did not understand it either. But we shall be able to explain this better when we talk about the organisation of Territorial Defence and about the home guard. The fact that some of the Muslims did have uniforms but did not put them on on that day follows from the testimony of Witness C, who said that his brother started to put on his uniform on that day but then gave up. Witness D, whose father was the leader of a group, says his younger son had the uniform. Another witness said that while fleeing, a person he knows put on a uniform and others wore uniforms sometimes. What is especially important, and we shall often refer to this witness in our statement, is the testimony of Witness V, who confirmed that he never had a uniform and he did not have it on the 16th of April, 1993; neither did he have it when he went to the war front against the Serbs. And this same witness who had command responsibilities and who is a Prosecution witness said that there were many Muslims wearing civilian clothes on the war front against the Serbs. Then there is Witness Z, who says that he did have a uniform at home but that he hid his uniform on the 16th of April, 1993. And finally, expert witness Asim Dzambasovic confirmed that there was a shortage of uniforms in the Muslim army, and that is why many soldiers did not have uniforms, either at home, when they were in the Territorial Defence, or when they went to the war front against the Serbs. One witness went so far as to say that not only were these people wearing civilian clothes on the war front, but they did not even have any kind of patches or any military insignia on their civilian clothes. So when we look at these testimonies by witnesses who are all Prosecution witnesses, then we can see that among the military-able men who were among the corpses in Ahmici, the fact that they were not wearing uniform is of no relevance whatsoever. The fact that there were no military facilities, in the traditional sense of the word, in Ahmici is something I have already mentioned. The expert witness, Asim Dzambasovic, said that the members of the Territorial Defence were located at their homes, and the existence of a military unit, a Muslim military unit in Ahmici, is also confirmed by Witness CD, who said that the members of the British Battalion were not aware of the fact that a Muslim military unit existed in Ahmici because they were obliged to report to UNPROFOR places where there were military units, and the military unit in Ahmici had not been registered, which is why members of BritBat say that there was no military unit in Ahmici. What in fact the departure of people who were located at home to the war front looked like is evident from the video which was shown here and which shows a person going from house to house collecting men. With regard to the membership of people from Ahmici, Abdulah Ahmic confirmed that people from Ahmici were part of the Muslim-Vitez Brigade or, as they called it, the 325th Mountain Brigade, which had an organised command, which sometimes organised military exercises. And there were no barracks in Ahmici, but this soldier slept in their homes. The testimony of Abdulah Ahmic is corroborated by a Defence witness, and this is the only Defence witness we are referring to, Gordana Cuic, who, after the 20th of October, saw a unit of Muslims with weapons going to a military exercise. And their leader was Fuad Berbic, who said he was not afraid because this was just an exercise. Witness L also confirmed that this was the 325th Mountain Brigade. What is of special interest to us is Witness V. Not the part of his testimony that started with the Prosecutor's examination, but rather the part of his testimony after he was shown his own diary, which he admitted was written by him. So this document has not been challenged. It's a document drawn up by Witness V before the 16th of April, and in his haste to leave his home, he left it behind, where it was found, and that is why it was available to be used in these proceedings. According to what is written in this document, it follows clearly that people from Ahmici went to the military review of the battalion, to a company review in Vrhovine; that Witness V was appointed squad commander. And when all this was said to him, he went so far as to say that he has such a bad memory for dates that he could say nothing about the establishment of the brigade or about the unit to which he belonged at the time in question. However, we are invoking not so much his testimony as his diary, which he admitted writing in his own hand. Not only was there a military unit, but this military unit also had a military radio station with which it was linked with a higher command. We regret not having an appropriate technical witness who could testify about the technical characteristics of this radio transmitter, but, according to our information, with an appropriate antenna, it, from the position where it was located, it could communicate with a corps command in Zenica. Therefore, they were very well connected; they had very good contacts with the corps command. Witness Y essentially said the same as Witness V, although unfortunately he did not keep a diary, or we did not have it, because we could have seen a lot if we had had it. This witness came from the brigade command to help in the final organisation of the unit or, rather, the company in Ahmici. He avoided saying that he was one of the commanders in Ahmici. However, when it was said that a telegram arrived with orders that the unit should raise its -- that he was present at the meetings where they discussed the defence lines, and he was also present at the meetings where it was decided that guards should be established as a security measure. The fact that the army of BH, quite apart from Ahmici, had strong forces on the territory of the Vitez municipality follows from the statement of the witness Charles McLeod. From his statement, it follows clearly that Colonel Blaskic himself was surprised by the strength of the counterattack by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this forceful counterattack, which led to the loss of some Croatian villages, could not have been mounted had they not been present in the area, since it is quite clear, and this was confirmed by expert witness Asim Dzambasovic, that the army of B and H lacked weapons. They had a shortage of weapons and, therefore, it was not very mobile. Although the infantry, at least from what we could read in the newspapers, was very good, it took a long time for the infantry to be moved from one area to another because this had to be done mostly on foot and not by vehicles. Another interesting statement is that by Charles McLeod. All this time we were talking about the unarmed village of Ahmici, but he expressly stated that he did not believe that the village of Ahmici was not defended, because all the other villages mentioned in the indictment were defended, defended successfully; not only that, but the Croatian parts of these villages were lost for the Croats, and it is his assessment that the defence of the village of Ahmici was inadequate. I believe that this witness is also a former officer of the British army, who at that time was a military observer, and as regards this fact, he has absolutely no reason not to tell the truth. This is all the more convincing because he made his statement not under the direct impression of the burnt-out village of Ahmici and the corpses there, which left such a deep impression on the members of the British Battalion who were there, as it would have made on any one of us had we been there. Therefore, we deny that this was an undefended village. Something should be said about the fact which the Prosecutor calls a surprise attack. I have already mentioned that my client cannot be charged with organising or preparing an attack, and I have said that this was not an undefended village. In the situation where the masters of war decided that war should begin, surprise, as a military skill, cannot be seen as going against any law of war. The fact that surprise is an essential factor in any military operation follows from the testimonies of all the witnesses who had any knowledge of what is and what is not permitted in war and what effects are aimed at in a war; Bryan Watters, Witness B, and Asim Dzambasovic also confirmed this. One of the basic rules of war is to surprise the adversary. The greater the surprise, the better the effects. We shall even go so far as to say that the Muslims did have indications that something was afoot but that they did not pay proper attention to these indications and that they did not prepare properly. We refer to the testimonies of Witness Esad Rizvanovic, Witness B, and especially the fact that at about 23.00, Captain Matthew Woolley arrived in the headquarters in Vitez and told the staff officers who were there that Colonel Blaskic was having meetings with numerous officers in uniform, and this should have been a clear indication to them that if the staff of a zone is having meetings at such a late hour, then early the following morning, which is when attacks usually start, something was going to happen. However, they were not cautious enough, and the only measures they undertook were to sleep together in one place, as if they could achieve something in this way in the line of defence, and the people in Ahmici were given orders to raise their combat readiness and so they doubled their guards. The fact that they doubled their guards was not a good response to the orders they were given, because when a unit is ordered to raise their combat readiness to the first degree, that means that the unit should be at their positions and that every member of the unit must be prepared to fire, on command, at the enemy. It is alleged that Zoran Kupreskic, in the period covered by the indictment, was a person who persecuted Muslims. I will not now list all the witnesses who confirmed precisely the opposite and who told us that in all three aspects of his life -- at home, at work, and in his leisure time -- he was not against Muslims but, on the contrary, that he socialised with them until the last moment, that he attended Bajram celebrations in Muslim houses in 1993, that he played at Bajram celebrations in Stari Vitez, but I shall only point out the fact that the only multiethnic society or group of people functioning in that way was the folklore group, of which the Kupreskic brothers were members. Therefore, even if there was pressure brought to bear on them to join a single ethnic society, they managed to oppose this -- and they suffered material damage because no one gave them any financial support because they were a multiethnic society -- then this shows that Zoran was never against a multiethnic cultural society and that he showed no tendencies of belittling, humiliating, or depriving anyone of their rights simply because they belonged to another race or religion. We have, during the course of the proceedings, provided ample evidence of this, so I don't think there's any need to go back to that. We come now to a more complicated issue, and that is whether Zoran Kupreskic was an HVO soldier before the crimes were committed. The Defence alleges that he was not. In his closing statement, the Prosecutor said something which does not exist anywhere in the world; he talks about an active reservist or a reserve activist -- I'm not quite sure which term he used -- but if somebody is active duty, he is not a reservist; if he is a reservist, he cannot be an active duty, because one notion excludes the other. There may be an error in the interpretation, but otherwise I don't know how such a concept can exist of an active reservist. Let me go on. A fact that the Prosecutor relies on is that Zoran Kupreskic took an oath of allegiance to an HVO military unit at the Vitez stadium, and he draws this conclusion from a statement made by Witness JJ. The simple matter of taking an oath, Your Honours, does not make a reservist an active-duty soldier, and it is even possible for a reservist to be called up to serve for a single day, and that for that day, he has to take an oath; and then after that day, he may be discharged and become a reservist again, until he is called up to serve once more. Therefore, the act of taking an oath is no evidence at all that, on the 16th of April, 1993, Zoran Kupreskic was an active-duty soldier. Zoran Kupreskic is aware of this fact, and it would not damage his defence if he had said, "I was present at the oath-taking because I was invited," or he might have put it in a different way: "If I had been called up, I would have gone." Because, as I said, this fact is quite irrelevant and doesn't prove that he was active. He was not there, as he said, for the simple reason that he was among the spectators, among the audience. The only evidence that Zoran Kupreskic was among those who took an oath is a statement by Witness JJ. I shall come back to her testimony, as she was supposed to be the witness for the Defence. However, in her testimony, there is a detail that is particularly interesting, and that is that she claims that she saw Zoran Kupreskic in line on a videotape. If she saw Zoran Kupreskic on a video, then either she or someone close to her must have that videotape, and if that videotape was in accordance with what she is alleging, then the Prosecutor would have shown that videotape to the Court, and I believe the witness would have given the Prosecutor that tape. If she didn't give him that tape, then that means that she reviewed the tape and she must have seen that Zoran Kupreskic was not on the tape, and this would quite disprove her allegations. The Defence was in a very difficult position regarding videotapes because, from the beginning, when we started the defence, we examined the videotapes we received from the Prosecutor and (redacted) (redacted). Had it not been for the Prosecutor, then we could have relied only on the TV programme. But that's another issue; I'll come back to that later. Therefore, we tried to get hold of that videotape, but we haven't managed to do so. But we're convinced that on that tape, Zoran Kupreskic is not shown in line. If we manage to get hold of it, we will show it to Your Honours. Furthermore, the Prosecutor relies on Witness JJ, who said that she knew that Zoran Kupreskic went to the front against the Serbs, and he also relies on the statement of Abdulah Ahmic, who said that he went to the front in Busovaca. Well, he couldn't have gone to both fronts at the same time, so one statement obviously contradicts the other. However, Abdulah Ahmic says what he really knows, and JJ what she doesn't know, from direct observation. That Zoran Kupreskic did not go to the front is best seen from the fact that he was working throughout that time. He had to work, because he was working on the maintenance of machines, and unless machines are maintained properly in a factory of dynamite and explosives, then there can be no proper production, nor can security of the personnel be ensured in the factory, because various accidents could occur as a result of faulty equipment. That Zoran Kupreskic was constantly employed follows not only from his testimony but also from the testimony of witness Ivan Taraba, who said that he worked in the department of maintenance and that he had one intermission of three weeks in June 1992, which is a period not covered by the indictment, when nobody even dreamt that a Croat or Muslim conflict would break out. As for the lineup at the stadium and the absence of Zoran Kupreskic from work, it is interesting to note that not a single witness called by the Prosecution could confirm the fact that Zoran Kupreskic was either absent from work or was present in the lineup. An important element of the Prosecutor's submissions that Zoran Kupreskic was an active reservist of the HVO is the list of members for 1992, covering a period from 1992 to 1996, and we should like to draw attention to the following: Regarding the dates, regarding the evaluation of certain documents, rather, I beg your pardon, the date when those documents were issued is important. If we look at this list that the Prosecutor is relying on, then we see that the list was compiled subsequently, after the end of the war, that the data entered are incorrect. We don't need to question witnesses or Zoran Kupreskic or any other witnesses, but it is sufficient to compare this document with documents issued at the time the content of the document is referring to. Thus, for instance, in the brief, you have a document on the discharge of Zoran Kupreskic -- and I refer to that exhibit in my brief, so I'm not going to mention the exhibit number -- and from this document, it is evident that he was not demobilised, as stated in the Prosecutor's document, but much earlier. Furthermore, the time of the beginning of his active involvement in the HVO, active involvement in the sense I understand it, is clearly stated in document P335, when the names of persons who were mobilised from the 16th of April to the 28th of April, 1993 are given. It is clearly stated there that Zoran Kupreskic was among the people who were mobilised in that time frame, so they could not have been mobilised on the 8th of April. So as to avoid any mistakes, we should like to underline that a person who, once he becomes an active soldier, is no longer remobilised; it is only civilians who are mobilised and not active military men. The witnesses who testified on this issue explain that the motive for incorrect data was to obtain certain benefits in the form of shares, with which it was possible to purchase dwellings; at least that was the idea. So the Croatian side did its best to extend the period of time as much as possible so that Croats would get as much material property on the basis of those shares as possible. However, I'm not referring only to the statements of Defence witnesses. I can also mention Prosecution Witness II, as a Muslim and a member of the Muslim army, alleges that similar things were applied on the Muslim side. So that the dates on the list for shares do not coincide with the real dates of participation in the army. The Prosecutor devotes attention to the question of the home guard regiment, and he said that the 92nd Home Guard Regiment existed at the time of the outbreak of the conflict, on the 16th of April, 1993, and he relies on the Official Gazette, ordering the formation of home guard units, and an act in March 1993 appointing the provisional command of the home guard regiment. Your Honours, the evidence presented by the Prosecution as evidence of the existence of a home guard unit are accurate on paper, but in reality are dead letter on paper, as were many other things in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the first place, if, in mid-March, the provisional command of the home guard regiment was appointed, it is not possible to organise such a regiment within a month, to make it a proper unit with officers, non-commissioned officers, headquarters, staffs, et cetera. Furthermore, if a home guard regiment had existed, and that is a unit of some strength, then that unit, on the 16th of April, would have received orders to do something; it would not have been sleeping in their beds. But Colonel Blaskic would have, in his orders which you have in the brief and which were issued from the 15th of March, in the afternoon, until the 16th of April, at 1.30, would have conveyed a part of the combat duties to that home guard regiment if it had existed. If it had been capable of offensive actions, then it would have been entrusted -- if it had not been capable of offensive actions, then it would have been given defensive actions to protect a particular village or a particular area. However, in Colonel Blaskic's commands, issued to all military units at his disposal, to even independent companies, such as military police companies, no mention is made of a home guard regiment, and this fact that the home guard regiment did not receive any kind of assignment is best proof that it did not exist. Furthermore, Your Honours, if a home guard regiment had existed, then the mobilised personnel would not have been assigned to the Vitez Brigade but to the home guard regiment. However, according to the report of the Defence Department in Novi Travnik, it can clearly be seen that mobilised personnel were assigned to the Vitez Brigade. So if such personnel were mobilised to the Vitez Brigade, surely there could not have been a home guard unit. And there were allegedly a provisional command who were killed as members of the Vitez Brigade. So that is all I have to say regarding the home guard unit. As far as the events of the 20th of October are concerned, in his closing argument the Prosecutor, as I have said, retraced his steps, and I have explained why. And it would be interesting for us to focus on the participation of Zoran Kupreskic in the negotiations on return -- on the return of people to their homes. First of all, he himself explained what he did and what his function was, rather, that he was a clerk. The Prosecutor did not disprove this allegation, nor did he try to disprove it through Witness Fuad Berbic, who he had at hand. And therefore, Your Honours, I believe that you will accept what Zoran Kupreskic himself said. When evaluating his testimony, please bear in mind that both he and his brother were refugees from Ahmici in connection with the events of the 20th of October, and that it was in his personal interest for the situation in the village to be brought back to normal so that both he and his brother, with their families, could return home. After all, he did go home with his brother when the Muslims returned home. So that is the best sign that all he did in the course of those negotiations, he did in good faith. As for the demand to the Muslims to surrender their weapons, which the Prosecutor highlighted in his closing arguments, Your Honours, you have had occasion to hear that such a demand was made; that some did surrender their weapons, but the majority did not; that afterwards they went for exercises armed; that they had arms on them on the 16th of April; and that Zoran Kupreskic, who saw them armed, never took any steps to seize those arms. Something that I was particularly surprised by in the closing arguments of the Prosecutor was the question of personal responsibility for the agreement reached between the two parties. This position regarding personal responsibility, when it is not a personal contract, never existed. And it seems to me that the Prosecution is trying to engage in some kind of an experiment for the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which has not succeeded anywhere. For instance, if we were to accept the Prosecutor's position that an interstate agreement, which may be signed by Peter and Paul as the government representatives, if that government were to lose its mandate, and if Peter were no longer Prime Minister, but somebody else, then the Prosecutor from this case would call Peter to account as to why he is not respecting that agreement. So I think that such a position on the part of the Prosecutor is quite unacceptable and is not applied anywhere in the world. We now have the contract on anti-ballistic missiles, for instance, so I think there is no need to dwell on this point. Furthermore, when, on the 20th of October -- or rather, the 21st of October, that agreement was being drafted, it never even occurred to anyone as to what would happen on the 16th of April, because in those days, in October, one would have to be a sorcerer to guess what would happen in April. I think even the warlords didn't know that that would happen, not to mention Zoran Kupreskic, a villager in a border area with the Muslims. So therefore such attachment of personal responsibility is absolutely out of the question. Furthermore, if we say that there was an agreement between two sides, then the agreement as a whole should be observed. Not a single letter was implemented, for instance, that all the Muslims should surrender their weapons. This is admitted by the Muslims themselves. Then there was no provision to form a joint military -- was not respected to form a joint military unit. Then also joint checkpoints at the road leading to Ahmici was also not implemented. And after all, Zoran Kupreskic was not a person writing lists of home -- of village guards, so he cannot be expected to have had any influence regarding the implementation of commitments regarding the protection of the Muslims of Ahmici. From the Defence of Zoran Kupreskic, confirmed by Witness Vidovic, it is clear that at the end of January or the beginning of February, the duty of coordinator of village guards was handed over to Dragan Vidovic; therefore, he no longer had absolutely any influence on the events, not even with respect to village guards. As for the time when he was the coordinator of those guards, there were no incidents. But village guards did not provoke anything. These things were provoked by outside units, which is something the Prosecutor recognises in his closing argument when he said who carried out which acts. He knows exactly which unit was in charge of protecting the road and which unit reported to General Blaskic on his operations in the area of Ahmici. I am not going to go from one witness to another, because I see that my time seems to be running up. And I think that we have to exercise discipline in order to leave enough time for our colleagues. So I'll try to shorten my part. I would like to dwell a bit on the question of Zoran Kupreskic, commander. This thesis about him being a commander is one that was also propounded by the Prosecutor, which is also partly based on Witness JJ's testimony. When speaking of commanders, and the Prosecutor says that Zoran Kupreskic was a commander, we should define first and foremost what a commander is. One can be a commander of a fire brigade, one can be a commander of a civil defence unit, of a police station, a prison, a work brigade, but also in the army as well. If we are to proceed from command within an army, then one can be a commander at various levels; of a squad, of a platoon, of a company, et cetera, going all the way up to an army. So the very fact that someone is a commander, without saying a commander of what, is meaningless. Zoran Kupreskic could not have been the commander of a military unit, not even of the smallest one. And this is shown by the fact that he was not in the army until the 16th of April, which is what I already talked about. That is quite obvious from the document that spoke about persons who were mobilised in the period between the 16th of April and later dates. Now, since it is a question of Witness JJ's testimony altogether, we have to point out that her statement in that part is a result of her concentration on her very own problems, and she had quite a few of them at the time. And we are not objecting to that, because she really was burdened with a great many problems. However, the fact that she was burdened by so many problems resulted in the fact that she did not exactly remember what the ID said and in which order and how. We have made every effort to obtain this document, this ID, but we haven't managed to do so, so far, but we hope that we will manage to do so after all. The witness does not have a very good memory, because she says that she can't even remember whether there was a photograph on the ID or not, and there is a photograph on every ID. She does not recall any photograph on the ID, and a document without a photograph cannot really be an ID. And this document is claimed to have been an ID. In addition to that, she said that next to Zoran Kupreskic's name it said "COMMANDER," in block letters. And that is quite incredible. As I said, there are different levels of command. So if the bearer of an ID was supposed to be identified as a person who does exercise command duties, then one had to state a commander of what. It is possible that Witness JJ got a bit confused with regard to what the ID said. She got things confused because she linked the word "commander" with the name of Zoran Kupreskic. And the word "commander" was in the lower bottom part where the name of the person who issued the ID is noted. Then it says commander so-and-so and then the signature of the person who is authorised to issue such an ID. And then there is also a seal of the relevant institution that issued the ID next to the name and title of that person. So we still claim that the word "commander" was not written next to Zoran Kupreskic's name. If it were put next to a name and surname, then that kind of an ID would have been dangerous for the bearer of that ID. Whoever is vaguely familiar with the customs of war knows that in dangerous situations command posts and command duties are concealed for persons who are in dangerous situations. And to state in an ID that someone is a commander would seriously jeopardise his position if he were to be taken prisoner by the other side, because then the other side would know immediately who they have in their hands. And everybody tries to avoid that kind of a situation. In addition to that, Your Honours, Zoran Kupreskic was no commander in the time that the Prosecutor mentioned, and that is proven by yet another document that was shown to us by the Prosecutor. That was the recommendation issued in the autumn of 1993, to have Zoran Kupreskic promoted to officer's rank. Had Zoran Kupreskic been at the battlefield at the front before that? Had he been among any persons who passed any kind of military or civilian decisions? Had he been the commander of anything, even of a villager's cooperative? Then in the recommendation for his promotion to officer's rank, that fact would have been highlighted; that would have been an essential element for having what is being proposed materialised, and that is for him to become an officer. This is document D21/1, and that is the document we got from the Prosecutor, and it shows quite clearly that at the very beginning he was not a supporter of the prevailing politics of that time at all; he joined in only later, when the war between the Croats and the Muslims was already raging, and there was no other option for him but to join the Croat side in the war. So through that document -- well, I don't know. Perhaps this is a question of procedure. But in our legal system, the Prosecutor sometimes says a kind word or two about the accused as well, but anyway. As for the substance of the conversation that Zoran Kupreskic had with Witness JJ, she got some of the things mentioned confused in that respect as well. She states, for example, that Zoran Kupreskic said that he was some kind of a commander and the like, but also that he said that he was assigning people to guard duty in the part of the village where he lived. Since you have the opportunity of seeing and hearing Witness JJ, you managed to see for yourselves that she says a lot on the basis of what she deduces on her own, rather than speaking about facts. When she was asked why she thought he was a commander, she said that she thought so because he was making lists, assigning people to guard duty. However, what is important is that she confirmed that Zoran told her that his -- that he managed to get rid of that duty; that is to say, making lists of people who would go on guard duty, that he managed to get rid of that a lot earlier. So in case of witnesses, one should draw a distinction between what they know and what they deduce. However, in the case of this particular witness, there are things that are related to her deduction and conclusions as well. She says, for example, that Zoran Kupreskic took part in some kind of negotiations a month before the 16th of April in terms of the removal of roadblocks that the Muslims put. Because Dario Kordic was supposed to come to Ahmici. No one, not a single witness from Ahmici, spoke of Dario Kordic's coming to Ahmici. So obviously again it's a question of her own conclusions, because somebody from Ahmici would have had to know about this; it would not have only been the lone statement of Witness JJ. There are other such examples. For example, the witness says that Zoran told her that he came -- that he went back to the trenches. However, no one, absolutely no one, either from the Croat or the Muslim side, confirmed that part of her statement, that in Ahmici there were any kind of trenches. As for all the Defence witnesses -- I'm sorry, Prosecution witnesses, they mentioned this for the first time in connection with the 18th of April, when they were brought to the front line in Pirici. So although we believe Witness JJ to a large extent, there are parts that do not fit into the true picture of events. As for the development of relations between Croats and Muslims, I wouldn't want to dwell on that specifically. However, it would be a good thing to mention here the difference between the Territorial Defence on the one hand and village guards on the other. The Prosecutor's approach to this problem is quite interesting. Everything that we had claimed that pertained to village guards, the Prosecutor says in respect of the Territorial Defence. In his closing arguments, although the Prosecutor's witness, the expert witness, Asim Dzambasovic, showed that the Territorial Defence was organised as a military structure with a general staff in Sarajevo, with the command centres of corps, with command posts in Vitez itself and with units that were organised according to the territorial principle, and the Muslim population was mobilised at that time, which can be seen from the order on mobilisation, which is also among the Defence exhibits. As opposed to the Territorial Defence, which is organised from a military point of view, with commanders, with military discipline, et cetera, the members of the village guards were those who guarded their homes with rifles and who were outside any kind of structures or chains of commands and were mobilised only after the war started, which can be seen from the list of mobilised persons that was mentioned so many times. So I don't really want to go back to all of that once again. Once again, this supports our thesis, that is to say, what the -- rather than what the Prosecutor has said. Asim Dzambasovic speaks in favour of what we have been proposing. I'm so glad to be able to invoke his statement on so many occasions because, indeed, he was impartial and objective. Now, for another thing, whether the Croats from Ahmici knew what would happen on the 16th of April, including Zoran Kupreskic. Your Honours, you have seen General Blaskic's orders; you have seen where these orders came from. You saw in all these orders that there was a clause stating "Military Secret - Strictly Confidential." If those orders say "Military Secret - Strictly Confidential," that means that the broad population cannot be aware of these orders. The fact that the population was not aware of this can be seen from various examples. For example, Ivica Kupreskic's wife came on the 15th of April to Ahmici, and on the 14th of April, she landed in Split, her plane from Germany landed in Split. She certainly would not have returned to Ahmici one day before the war started had she known that the war was about to break out. The same goes for the brother of Jozo Alilovic, whose name is Tomo Alilovic; he came from Germany too. When the war began, he was hiding, together with that other witness who came to Jozo Alilovic's, and he was afraid that he would be mobilised. Finally, the brother of Milutin Vidovic would not have spent the night between the 15th and 16th of April in Stari Vitez, and he would never return from there alive. As for the way in which this is being proven -- that is to say, that on the 15th of April, the Croats knew what would happen on the 16th of April -- the Prosecutor uses witness statements. Some of these witnesses show certain things superficially and only in part. Witness F is a case in point, and he was also mentioned by the Prosecutor in his closing argument; namely, Witness F mentioned that Ivica Kupreskic, on the 15th of April, 1993, in an automobile that was a Mercedes, which seems to be very important -- not a Fiat, heaven forbid -- and he was driving from his home to another place. And now he would have seen that Ivica Kupreskic had evacuated his wife and child because he knew that on the 16th of April there would be a war. His wife had come back from Germany, and he drove his wife to see her parents, to visit her mother. Then they all went back home and then all their neighbours came to say hello to her and to bid her welcome, and this was confirmed by all these neighbours. Witness F does not take this into account at all, and from what I can see, the Prosecutor doesn't take this into account either, and he only quotes Witness F in order to prove that Croats evacuated their women and children a day earlier. So that's quite nice, to quote such witnesses who say that, on the 15th of April, Croat children did not go to school. The Prosecution witness is that kind of a witness too, and he omits to mention that Witness H, who went to school herself, said the exact opposite; that is to say that all the Croat children came to school on the 15th of April, as usual. Therefore, we say that they did not know, nor could they have known, on the 15th of April, what would happen on the 16th of April. We say that only when he was awakened on the 16th of April did Zoran Kupreskic learn that something was happening; only then did he find out what he was told, and that was that families should be evacuated because a Muslim attack was imminent. Your Honours, in my final brief, I refer to events preceding the 15th, including the tragic event in Dusina, which was mentioned, quite properly, by the Prosecutor, where Mujahedin, not Muslim neighbours, killed a large number of Croats, and that in the minds of persons who knew about this, this was corroboration of the information that a Muslim attack was imminent. If you look at the orders issued by Colonel Blaskic, you will see that they were all issued on the basis of information he had received that a Muslim attack was imminent. I am not going into whether this information was correct or incorrect. It may have been incorrect; it may have been designed to prompt Colonel Blaskic to prepare his troops for action. But Colonel Blaskic had wider sources of information available to him, and he believed it, so why would Zoran Kupreskic not believe it, who had only one source of information which told him to evacuate his wife and children because there was an imminent Mujahedin attack? You should also realise that what the Prosecutor claims is absurd, that Zoran Kupreskic was to tell the Muslims that a Muslim attack against the Croats was about to happen. Because what kind of threat was there against the Muslims to make Zoran Kupreskic tell his Muslim neighbours that Muslims were about to attack the Croats? I have never heard anything so absurd in my life, and I believe you will not take this into consideration, because, of course, you are not going to tell the other side that they are about to attack you. So much for what the Prosecutor says about this. As regards the information people got, Zoran Kupreskic told you, in his defence, that the information broadcast in the media was contradictory because the Croats always said that it was the Muslims who were attacking, and vice versa, and the persons who listened to all this were confused. Someone listening to all this could not know what the truth actually was, and, in fact, we do not know certain things even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Counsel Radovic, your time is up; you were allocated an hour and a half. It's 10.30. We have now to take a break, a 20-minute break, and then it will be the turn of Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Part of what I have said refers to my colleague also. I would need at least 20 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but this will be taken, the 20 minutes, from the time allocated to Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. If she's agreeable, that's all right. We agreed that each Defence counsel, except for the Defence counsel for Dragan Papic, would be allocated an hour and a half, and that's our decision. So if Counsel Slokovic-Glumac is prepared to give you 20 minutes as a gift, why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We shall talk about this during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. A 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague has given me ten minutes, so I will try to make the best use of them. I will only speak about the Witness JJ, because she has been my favourite witness ever since I entered this case. This witness also shows the kind of problems the Defence came up against when trying to obtain witnesses not belonging to the same ethnic background. The first time I arrived in Vitez, I heard that JJ had been on friendly terms with Zoran Kupreskic, and there was no mention of their discussing what took place in Ahmici but only that she should confirm that Zoran Kupreskic helped her and her family after the 16th of April. Since I did not know her personally, and since there was a danger that my direct contact with her might be misunderstood, I made use of the fact that our witness, Ljiljana Sapina, was on friendly terms with her. So I sought contact with her through this witness, either that she should come to Vitez or that she should send us a written statement; there was even the possibility of Ms. Slokovic-Glumac and I going to Zenica and taking a statement from her there, in any premises she chose, either at the police station or the court or on the premises of a representative of the OTP. To begin with, she agreed. You saw the letter that the witness Ljiljana Sapina received, which is an exhibit in this case. However, the fact that she was subjected to various kinds of pressure is evident from her testimony. Somebody heard that she was to testify on behalf of the Defence, and she was told that this would not be wise and that it might have bad consequences for her. In the end, the witness told her friends that she had been required to testify and that she would never have consented to appear as a Defence witness otherwise, and then she started saying all kinds of nasty things about Zoran Kupreskic. We are very grateful to the Prosecutor for bringing her here as a witness, because he was successful in something that we had not managed to do. And I would like to ask you to bear this in mind when evaluating her testimony. And what part of her testimony is acceptable and what part is not is something I have already talked about. This is as far as the facts are concerned. Then I will not go into legal issues now. The final proposal of Zoran Kupreskic is that he should be fully acquitted. Since we are putting this proposal, we will not talk about mitigating circumstances. However, regardless of what your judgement is, Your Honours, we would like you to release Zoran Kupreskic on a temporary basis, because everything we have said so far in favour of his being released from detention is justified. In the meantime we have obtained guarantees from the Croatian component of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that should they not appear before the Court of their own accord, they will be handed over to SFOR. However, if they gave themselves up, if they came to The Hague of their own accord, even though they are far from any decision-making circles, there is no reason to suppose that they will not come here to hear their sentence. They have been separated from their families for two Christmases, two New Year holidays, and this is very hard on them because people in that part of the world are very attached to their families, and because of this fact they have been suffering for two years. We admit that these sufferings are far less than the sufferings of the Muslims who suffered in Ahmici and their families, but because they are not responsible for these sufferings, there is no reason not to release then. All the more so, as the President of the Court, of the Tribunal, according to the news we heard on Croatian radio when submitting her report to the security council about the work of the Tribunal, expressly stated that she would support the temporary release of persons who come to -- who give themselves up voluntarily and appear before the Court voluntarily. I thank you for this extension and I now give the floor to my colleague. I have not exceeded the ten minutes that she gave me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to begin with, with regard to the Prosecutor's statements yesterday, I have a few comments. He said that Zeljo Livancic was probably a member of the military police, and I would like to say that this is incorrect. And this is evident from Exhibit 35353. Zeljo Livancic is not on the list of persons killed as members of the military police. He was a member of the Vitez Brigade. Furthermore, the Prosecutor said that Dragan Vidovic transmitted orders and that he said that Zeljo Livancic transmitted orders at the civil defence meeting in the night of the 16th of April. And this is also incorrect. He also said that the Jokers could not have attacked Ahmici on their own. This is not what we are saying. We consider that the military police participated in the attack on Ahmici, so we are not talking about a Joker squad consisting of 30 or 40 people, but of the whole battalion, the 4th Battalion of the military police. And this follows from the testimony we heard before this Tribunal, according to which Mirjan Santic was a member of the 2nd Platoon of the military police, which was the traffic police. Apart from this, to a direct question of the President of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecutor said he did not know where Mirjan Santic was killed. We submitted to this Court Exhibit D25/1, from which it is evident that Mirjan Santic was killed in Ahmici on the 16th of April during the MOS attack on the defence line. We also submitted an extract from the record of death for Zlatko Ivankovic, who was killed on the 16th of April, 1993 in Ahmici as a member of the military police. We submitted D89/2, which is an extract from the record of deaths for Ivica Zepackic, who was also killed on that day as a member of the military police. Zeljko Arapovic and Slavko Rajkovic were also killed on the same day as members of the military police. So this is our response to the Prosecutor's claim that only villagers of Ahmici were killed on that day, which is not true. As regards the status of Mirjan Kupreskic, who, according to the Prosecution, was a soldier of the HVO. My colleague, Mr. Radovic, referred to this on a number of occasions. He was a member of the village guard, and there is nothing other than this in the file. He held a job until the outbreak of the conflict on the 15th of April, 1993, and P335 shows that Mirjan Kupreskic was mobilised in the period between the 16th and the 28th of April. Furthermore, Mirjan Kupreskic was seen carrying weapons in Ahmici by one single person before the conflict broke out, and this is a person who testified before this Tribunal under the pseudonym Z. And he said that he saw him on the roadblock which was set up at the entrance to Ahmici after the first conflict. So no other person says that they saw Mirjan Kupreskic with weapons before the conflict broke out. The roadblock was set up for only one reason, and this was at the orders of the Muslim and the Croatian political leadership, and it was a joint roadblock. Furthermore, the Prosecutor said that numerous witnesses saw Mirjan Kupreskic in uniform carrying weapons. We have heard only one witness testify to this -- or, rather, two witnesses, S and X, who said that they saw him in uniform on several occasions when he went to keep guard in the village guards. Now, it follows from the testimony of members of the Vitez Brigade that there were no members of the Vitez Brigade in Ahmici and Pirici on the 14th of April. From the list of HVO members in Novi Travnik dated 22nd February 1993, it is evident that Mirjan Kupreskic was not on this list. The Prosecutor in his final letter claims that the village guards were linked up among themselves horizontally, and that they were vertically linked to the HVO structure. As proof that this is so, the Prosecutor uses the thesis that the roadblock was set up on the 20th of October, 1992, as testified to by Witness B, who says that Dragan Cerkez set up this roadblock. This was wartime conflict. It was an exceptional situation; it was not the regular state of affairs. I apologise. The second matter referred to by the Prosecutor, when he wants to show the vertical connection with what the HVO is, that the guards in Donja Rovna were organised in a different way, and Zoran Santic spoke of this. They were to guard Radak's bridge from the HVO in Busovaca before the 16th of April. However, this is not proof of a vertical connection. It is proof that in that part the village guards were organised in a different way for a single reason, and that was that the war in Busovaca had been going on for two months. So the village guards were already well established, and we know that in Busovaca the war started on the 25th of January. The Prosecutor says that it is very strange that the Kupreskic brothers did not have military booklets, because he considers that they would contain important data. However, these booklets do not have the significance that the Prosecutor attaches to them, first of all, because the administration lagged behind the actual situation to a great extent, and the military booklet was a document used in times of peace to enter data about a soldier, and of course it could not be used during military operations. I should also like to say that not a single witness at this trial said that he had seen Mirjan Kupreskic going to the front line, attending military exercises, or undertaking any kind of military action. So all the allegations of the Prosecutor can be reduced to the testimony of two witnesses. With respect to the factual allegations made by the Prosecutor regarding persecution, colleague Radovic has already referred to this, but I should like to say in addition that the allegation of the Prosecutor that Mirjan Kupreskic had organised HVO soldiers, weapons and ammunition in Ahmici and Santici is also incorrect. Several witnesses, like Witness V, said that he saw five or six soldiers at the crossroads in front of the Kupreskic houses the day before the attack. He didn't say that he saw among them either Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic. Also, the allegation of the Prosecutor has not been proven; that is that Mirjan Kupreskic had evacuated the Bosnian Croats the night before. All he did was to take his family away in the morning, deep within the Croatian part of Santici, where they were partially protected, for the simple reason that the house of his father was on the borderline between the Croatian and Muslim part of the village. As for receiving reports that the Muslims were about to attack, the Kupreskics had earlier on had problems and had had to leave their houses, and so they accepted this report without thinking about it, and sought to take their families to a safer place. Mirjan Kupreskic received the report about the attack early in the morning on the 16th of April. The only information he had, had to do with the attack of Mujahedins, that is, the Muslims. As this was a Muslim attack, naturally their attack could only have focused on the Croatian population. Another question that arises is whether the information they received was true. If we look at the orders of Colonel Blaskic and compare them with the report which has been tendered as D16/2 -- Mr. President, I don't know whether perhaps we should go into private session for me to read the first paragraph only of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, we submit that no attack was ordered and that all General Blaskic's orders do not mention anywhere any order to attack Ahmici. This report shows what the results of that were. The Prosecutor says that the Croats actually had no reason to believe this report that the Muslims were about to attack, firstly, because allegedly there were no Mujahedins; then also because Croatia was on the offensive and as Ahmici was a Muslim village. Those allegations do not stand. In the first place, there were Mujahedins, and we have heard testimony about their operations on a number of occasions. Even the Muslims themselves, when they spoke about extremist segments of the Muslim army, used that term. Secondly, Croatia was not in an offensive of any kind at the time. Croatia or, rather, the Bosnian Croats of Central Bosnia were in a position to be exposed to attacks by the Muslim army. Just before this attack there were several incidents, and this situation was extremely tense because of those incidents. Among those incidents, some are mentioned in ECMM reports, and we heard reference to some of them by witnesses. To say that Ahmici was a particular target because it was a majority minimum population, that is also not true, because there were many Muslim villages in the surroundings, some purely Muslim, and in that respect, Ahmici was not special in any sense. As for the defence of the accused, Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic tell us that they spent the whole day in a depression next to their house, that they were in an area that was strategically not ideal, but it was close to the shelter where their families were, and they spent the whole day there, together with other people whom we called as Defence witnesses. The Prosecutor also submits that this was a strategically poor position and that there was no reason for them to stay there, that there was no reason for them to stay there after their families had left. In the first place, that depression may have been a poor or a good strategic position, but that is something they didn't think about. It was a place where they would seek shelter as a matter of habit, and at least they were protected from infantry weapons. Furthermore, they were able to see what was happening on the roads leading to Niko Sakic's house, where there was a shelter, and the road leading to the shelters where their families were accommodated. Furthermore, they were not far from their families. All the families were in one place, down the road leading out of the depression. The fact that they stayed on after their families had left for Rovna does not mean much because, actually, they just spent the night there, and then the next morning, as we know, they were mobilised and taken to Pirici. Also, the family of Zoran Kupreskic stayed in the same place, in Milutin Vidovic's house, until they were transferred to Vitez. The Prosecutor, in his closing argument, relies mostly on three witnesses. The first is Witness C, who saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic on the day of the attack, that is, the 16th of April, around noon, in the Alilovic house. That witness at the time was 13 years old, and according to his allegation, that day, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic came with some other soldiers, and in the words of Jozo Alilovic, which he said to Witness C, they had come for a drink. In describing those events, the witness adds greenish ribbons on the sleeves of the soldiers, and these greenish ribbons were mentioned for the first time in court. Before that, they were never mentioned, and they were obviously an indication of membership in a combat unit. The witness also mixes the names of the people who were with Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic on that day, and clearly the witness does not know Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. In court, first, he could not remember the name of Mirjan Kupreskic, and then during the identification, he mixed them up. Furthermore, a day or two before the identification, the Prosecutor had shown the witness pictures of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. So we feel that this identification process is unacceptable. The allegation of the witness that he knows Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic well, for more than eight years, is also incorrect. If he had known them for so long, surely he would not have forgotten the name of Mirjan Kupreskic, nor would he have confused their identity. The position from which this witness was viewing the scene of entry of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic in the house is also questionable. He says he was in another house, saying that he was in hiding, and, peeping through, he saw a group of soldiers, among whom was Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. The Prosecutor also said that he doesn't know the reason why Witness C would charge Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic; however, on the 2nd of May, 1993, this witness said that Zoran Kupreskic had wounded his father on his way back from a mosque, that he had thrown a grenade at the house of Zahid Ahmet and Mirsad Ahmic, when he killed three children and Mirsad Ahmic's wife. So this is obviously a story the witness had heard, and he tried to fit into that story, out of his own motives, obviously motives of revenge, to include Zoran Kupreskic. Usually, when the name of Zoran Kupreskic is mentioned in these proceedings, the next name to be mentioned is Mirjan Kupreskic, and then come all the others. Jozo Alilovic was heard as a witness, and he denied that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were in his house on that day. Also, this witness alleges that he saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic in camouflage uniforms on that day, that their faces were clean, without any paint on them, as opposed to witnesses who are charged with crimes in other houses, who say that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were wearing black uniforms on that day and that they had paint on their faces, which was either black or in different colours. Therefore, can this witness be trusted, or the other witnesses? It is up to Your Honours to judge. In any event, it is impossible, as the Prosecutor claims, that those attackers changed their clothing in the course of the day. With respect to the event in the house of Witness KL, an event referred to in Counts 2 to 12 of the indictment, the Prosecutor called one witness, Witness KL, who, in his testimony in court, said that on the 16th of April, 1993, in the morning, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic entered his house and they killed all the members of his family. The Defence denies the truthfulness of the testimony of this witness regarding the events that took place in his house and claims that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were not in his house on that day, nor did they commit the crimes of which they are charged. In the first place, the Defence has received eight statements by Witness KL, and from those statements, it is evident that the witness described all critical events in one way in court and in a significantly different way in the statements. These have to do with significant aspects of the act, and, therefore, one may rightly call in question the credibility of the witness and the truthfulness of his testimony. This witness, in the first place, made a whole series of statements containing elements which are contradictory, as admitted by the Prosecutor. First, regarding the identity of the perpetrators of the act, he changed his story, first saying that they were unknown people, and ending up by actually accusing Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. Also, he changed his testimony as to why he did not immediately reveal the names of the perpetrators. He first said that he wasn't asked, then that it didn't occur to him, and finally he came out with the reason that he was afraid. Because of the differences in describing the perpetrators, he starts by saying that uniformed men, with caps on their heads, or rather black hoods with openings for the eyes, had come into his house. After repeating this statement, he ends up by saying that the perpetrators had only black paint on their faces. Apart from changing the description of the attackers, he also changes the position from which he observed the attackers. In several of his initial statements, he said he was in the next-door room, that he had opened the door ajar, and that he was peeping through; then he said that he hid behind the couch in the front room and that he was an eyewitness of the killing of his son, daughter-in-law, and children from another room. The Prosecutor said that there was mention of a sofa, but this is in another room. So this does not confirm the consistency of the witness's statement but, rather, the opposite. Finally, in his statement for the investigating judge and the investigator of the ICTY, and in court here, the witness said that he was in the same room in which the murders were committed. The witness also differently describes the events that occurred in that house by giving different times as to when he fell behind the couch and also giving different times as to when his son and daughter-in-law were killed and what and who he saw. Also, his statements differ as to who was shooting, who set fire to the house, and in what way the attackers had entered the house. In describing the weapon, again there are differences. Firstly, he said it was a rifle, an MGV, with a classical barrel containing the ammunition, and in court, he admits that the rifle could have been larger. But there is no larger rifle with such a classical type of barrel. Also, the Defence submits that the differences in the statements were not due to his own errors but is evidence of the fact that the witness regularly and systematically changed his testimony. The witness begins by making a statement immediately following the events, and the statements given in the first 20 or so days following the events are obviously the closest to the truth. At that time, he was interviewed by Zenica Television and the State Security Service, and he spoke to Witness HH in that period. The contents of those statements are identical, because the witness describes the event by saying that he was in the next-door room and he was peeping through a door that was ajar and that he rather heard, than saw, what was happening in the room. He described the attackers as HVO soldiers or, rather, persons masked with caps over their faces. After that, the witness changed his statement, and substantially so. Now he tried to put himself in the following position, that he could recognise the perpetrators of the act. He could not have recognised them from the room where he was because, as he was hiding behind the couch, he could not have seen what was going on in the room. If he was peeking through the door that was only ajar, he could not have seen what was going on in the room; he could only have seen a small fragment of the room. Then the witness changed his own position. He said that during the attack he was in the room or, rather, by the door to the room. That is how he was in a position to see the attacker as well, but at that point, the attacker saw him too. According to his statement, these were persons who were shooting at a baby in a cradle. Then he would have had to have been a victim of this attack too. It is illogical that all persons in that house were killed and he was the only one who survived, while being in the same room. It is for that reason that, for the first time, the witness said that when the attacker charged towards him, he fell. Since he was not even grazed by a bullet when three bursts of gunfire were shot at him, he must have had a good shelter, and the shelter was the couch, and that is how the person, the attacker who was shooting, missed him.
