That is the first time that he mentioned that he was in the room and that he was shot at and that he fell. In the statement he gave to the police in Zenica, he said that (redacted) was sleeping on the bed with her son (redacted) and that the attacker shot at both of them. After that, when making a statement to the investigating judge, he said that (redacted) was sleeping on the couch. Obviously, he needed this couch in order to protect himself. During the trial, he insisted on the couch and said that he never had said earlier on that the child had slept anywhere else. He did not only move himself in terms of the position where he was. The witness, in order to be in a position to identify the attackers, had to see their faces, at least to a certain extent. That is why he had to change the original description of the attackers. The attackers were masked by balaclavas at the time. Finally, the witness described the attackers as persons without any caps and that they were only masked with a few markings on their face. So in a few statements, the witness changed his testimony completely. He was getting closer and closer to the attackers and their faces were becoming more and more recognisable. The witness's statement changed profoundly thereby. There was an attempt of murder, then in terms of whether the attacker fell or not, where the child slept, et cetera. And all these elements serve one purpose, and that is to say, make the witness's statement convincing in terms of recognising the attackers. In addition to all these other changes which bring into question the credibility of the witness, the witness makes mistakes while giving evidence. He makes mistakes in terms of the action taken by the attackers. He makes mistakes in terms of describing the action related to their entry into the room. He makes mistakes in terms of describing the attack itself. The reason why he is doing this is only one, and that is that the witness was not present while this event occurred, so he was not sure in terms of what he was saying. He repeated something that he had said before. He changed other things. And that is all how all this confusion was created. Characteristic is his lack of certainty with regard to the weapons that the attacks had. He started with a MGV machine-gun. After it was ascertained that this machine-gun uses 0.22-millimetre ammunition, that is to say, ammunition for a pistol, and after it was also established that on site, bullet casings were found of a .76 calibre that are used by a Kalasikov, and this was also the result of expert findings, Kerkhoff, and this was admitted as P170, the witness allowed for the possibility of a bigger rifle. Also, during the trial there was a noticeable difference in terms of how and with what degree of certainty the witness spoke about various events. While he described the events after leaving the house, he was sure of himself, reasonable, and he was in a position to repeat the sequence of events. However, before that, and while he was talking about events in the house, as I already mentioned, he made a series of mistakes. There is another very important detail which points to the fact that the witness perhaps had not even been in the room next door during these events. When he made his statement to Witness HH, he did not know whether the children had been killed before they were burned. The witness could not say -- that is to say that he did not even know what had happened to the children. There was also the possibility of the witness having slept downstairs in the basement, where he would spend a lot of time. When he heard detonations and shots early in the morning, he ran away and hid in the barn; and later, when the barn was torched, he was burned himself. There is another thing that speaks in favour of this. When the witness came to his mother's place in Pirici, he heard shots and he fled. He left his mother behind. And she was later saved by Ljubo Vidovic, also a witness. A man who was a witness of the killing of children, could he have left his mother at the mercy of such persons? The testimony of Ljubo Vidovic speaks in favour of this as well. She said that the witness's mother said that her son had saved himself by running away from the house, and that he was burned while hiding in the hay. So a lot of this is illogical and unconvincing. It is illogical that an attacker would shoot three bursts of gunfire at a one-metre distance into the person without even having a single bullet graze him. Secondly, the fact that the attacker would shoot from the handle of the couch without even noticing this himself. Also it is illogical that only one attacker would have weapons, and it is a house that was being attacked, where they did not know who would be there. Also, if we disregard all the previous statements made by this witness, what is also doubtful is the way in which he says he recognised Mirjan Kupreskic. The witness says that Mirjan Kupreskic entered the room, crouching, leaning forward, and allegedly right behind Zoran, who came in first. He saw another person dimly, in a haze, because he was concentrated on the first attacker, who was shooting. If this is an event which lasted for a few moments only, as the witness pointed out on several occasions; if the other attacker walks in while crouching and leaning forward, behind the first attacker, and they are entering practically simultaneously; and if the witness is focused on the first attacker, because that's the one who is shooting; and if he sees the other one only in a haze and only for a minute; and if the attackers are masked, how is it possible for the witness to be so certain of the identity of the person whom he saw? The Defence believes that this is not possible, and that the witness came to his own conclusions with regard to the identity of the attackers and not by way of direct observation. As for the events that took place in Witness H's house, the Court heard Witness H, who, in her statements, also on several occasions made statements that were contradictory or mutually contradictory or contradictory to the statements that were previously given to the investigating judge. First of all, she denied having made any kind of a statement to an investigating judge, and then she changed her testimony once again to a large extent, compared to the statement made to the investigating judge. First of all, crucial elements where she changed her statement were the following: First of all, she said that her father did not have a rifle, that her father's name was mentioned, and before that she had not said that. Then she said that she kneeled before Zoran Kupreskic, that she begged him that they -- that he did not kill them. And before that she mentioned, during the investigation, the name of another soldier also during the investigation. She said that she saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic upstairs in the house as they were torching it, and then during the trial she said that she did not go upstairs. And then the question is how well this witness knows Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic. During the trial she said that she often saw Zoran Kupreskic in the store where he worked. This points to the fact that she did not really know Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic very well. Namely, Zoran Kupreskic never worked in the shop; it was Mirjan Kupreskic who worked in the shop in the village. Apart from him, there was another person who worked there. That was Ivica Tolic. The witness did not only confuse Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic. After getting out of the shelter, she said that she saw Mirjan Kupreskic on the staircase, but she did not mention him as a person whom she recognised as having worked in the shop before. In addition to that, she said that she saw Mirjan Kupreskic in the hall for a split second, in the house where the lights were dimmed, because there were no lights on in her house. And the entire event was happening under very traumatising circumstances; that is to say, at half past five in the morning. She saw him for a split second, she saw him masked, and she said that she undeniably recognised him. Because of certain statements that this witness gave, the Defence insisted that her mother be heard here; that is to say, Witness SA. However, in view of the condition of her health, she was not heard, and the Defence believes that this ruling of the Court has damaged the Defence. Namely, her mother, in a way -- could have been a statement that would have been a good check for the statement of Witness H. She said in her statement that all the persons who were in the house were in camouflage uniforms, with caps on their heads, and that they had various colours painted on their faces. Also, she said that all the soldiers were armed with pistols, knives and bombs, whereas her daughter talks about Zoljas and automatic rifles. Also, her daughter described these persons as persons in black uniforms, with black markings on their faces. Witness SA says that when she got out of the shelter in the children's room, there was no one. There were no soldiers there. And in the hall there was one soldier in camouflage uniform with various colours painted on his face. Witness SA did not recognise that person. However, Witness H, as opposed to her mother, says that after getting out of the shelter in the children's room, she saw Zoran Kupreskic, and then in the hall she saw Mirjan Kupreskic. Her mother, who was in the same situation that she was in, because they were getting out of the shelter together, recognised Mirjan Kupreskic as being the other person; that is to say, the person -- the soldier who was standing in the kitchen and who was rummaging through cupboards in a black uniform and with paint on his face. So one witness saw Zoran Kupreskic in the children's room and the other one said that there were no soldiers in that room. One saw Mirjan Kupreskic as a soldier who was in the hall and the other one recognised him as the soldier who was in the living-room. Both of them described the uniforms, but they did so differently. If we take into account the fact that the mother of the witness is closer to the generation of the accused and she knew her neighbours better, then it is surprising that she did not recognise them. Her later statement, when she says that she recognised Zoran, Mirjan and Vlatko in that house, is absolutely incredible and cannot be taken into account. Witness SA, in the second statement she gave, said that her daughter recognised Zoran Kupreskic, but for herself she said that she did not recognise anyone. However, in her statements, this witness never said that her daughter recognised Mirjan Kupreskic. Therefore, Mirjan Kupreskic is first mentioned in this case as a perpetrator of a crime in the house of Sukrija Ahmic, in the statement that Witness H gave to the investigating judge in Zenica on the 17th of December, '93, and then in the statement of her mother on the 20th of December, 1993, which means eight months after the event itself. After that, Witness KL also mentions him as the perpetrator of the crime in his house, but this was 10 months after the actual event. There is another important thing in terms of comparing the statements of Witness H and her mother, respectively, and that is that everything that Witness H said that she had done herself -- that is to say that she talked to the soldiers, that she answered questions; that she begged they be allowed to remain in shelter -- her mother says that she did all of that herself. So they give identical statements with regard to that part. Witness H also says that they got out of the shelter themselves; that is to say that they were not found in the shelter, that they came out of their own accord, whereas as her daughter stated something else. That is to say that all these persons are members of the same family, the family that suffered a great deal on the 16th of April, 1993. Witness KL is Witness H's grandfather. There is no doubt that they talked about these events, they influenced one another, and formed certain joint opinions. The last statement made by KL coincides to a large extent with the statement made by Witness H; that is to say, in terms of the attire of the attackers, the colour on their faces, the way in which their faces were painted, et cetera. Witness SA, who is the mother of Witness H, also tries to get closer to that story, although until she made a statement to the investigator of the ICTY, she kept saying that these were unknown persons in camouflage uniforms. Nevertheless, she changed her statement, and among all the persons present in the house and wearing camouflage uniforms, finally she saw two black uniforms, the uniforms of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic respectively. Also, Witness EE, who is the daughter of Witness KL, made several different statements. As for the commission of the crime in her house, she charged several persons with that, and I believe that the Prosecutor was convinced that these persons were not in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. However, this witness inter alia gave a statement to the police on the 14th of May, 1993, in which she mentioned that (redacted), during the first visit to the hospital, said that he was not in the room where his family had been killed, but that he was peeking through the door that was ajar. As for the place where (redacted) was during the time of the attack, corresponds to the description of the location that he gave in his first statements. In the same statement, she also mentioned that Witness SA said to her that her husband had been killed by Vlatko and Ivica Kupreskic and her house torched as well. Witness B is also a member of this family. He was an intelligence officer. What reasons would lead this family to accuse their neighbours of these murders? There is no doubt that this family suffered greatly on that day, and that they began to discover the perpetrators only later. In the case of Mirjan Kupreskic, this happened only in December 1993. They were certainly very frustrated because the perpetrators were not known, so they tried to conclude who the perpetrators might have been. The Kupreskics were their next-door neighbours. Their houses were closest to the houses of the victims. A gunfire came from the direction of their houses, so it was normal to conclude that if gunfire came from the direction of a certain house, it was the owners who fired. The houses of these people were not damaged and their families were not harmed. They thought that these were people who were respected in the village. So it was easy to conclude that all the Kupreskics were to blame and were to be accused of the crimes in their part of the village. However, it is characteristic that all these people do not mention the Kupreskics in their first statements, but only later on, and gradually. In their statements to the Ministry of the Interior, both Witnesses K and SL, listing the persons they thought might be responsible, did not mention either Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic. In this connection, and speaking of problems of identification, expert witness Professor Wagenaar said that every information which is not received in a completely clear way leads to its reprocessing, and in a certain way it is always subject to further knowledge gained by a witness. In the light of this testimony, we must point out that both witnesses who accuse Mirjan Kupreskic describe in their statements the circumstances in which they saw the accused. One saw them very vaguely, focusing in on someone else, and the other one only for a split second in a dark house. So there is no doubt that the information they received was not clear. With regard to the fact that the perpetrators were masked -- and this is something that all the witnesses say, and all their initial statements were to the effect that the persons who entered the house were masked either with balaclavas or paint -- it is interesting to note that a witness said that in the morning, at the very beginning of the conflict, the witness saw a group of soldiers coming down from the direction of Redzib Ahmic's house, in the direction of the houses of Huso Krslic, Meho Hrustanovic, and Sukrija Ahmic. Describing this group of soldiers, he said that they had some kind of winter caps on their heads which concealed their faces. It follows from this part of the testimony of Witness O that the group of soldiers coming from the direction of Redzib Ahmic's house and going towards the lower houses were wearing camouflage uniforms and carrying automatic rifles. This description corresponds to the first description given by Witness SA. Therefore, as regards this first group of witnesses, it should be pointed out that, due to their family connections and the essential differences in their statements, and because they changed their statements over the course of time, we consider them to be unreliable witnesses. The fact that Witness SA, according to the testimony of her daughter, Witness H, was in a state of shock does not mean that she was unable to see what kind of uniforms the attackers wore, what they looked like, and in what way or how they were armed. We can also see from her testimony that she was able to describe the sequence of events. It is my opinion, therefore, that the evidence presented to the Court as regards the alleged guilt of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic for the murders in the house of (redacted) and their participation in the murder of Sukrija Ahmic are not sufficient for a conviction. Therefore, I consider that the Prosecutor has not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the two of them perpetrated these crimes, since the application of the criterion of beyond reasonable doubt means that any rational hypothesis, except the hypothesis of guilt, must be ruled out. We consider that this evidence does not meet this criterion. Since we consider that the murders in the house of Witness KL, as alleged by the Prosecutor, have not been proved, and with relation to the events in the house of Sukrija, we consider that they do not correspond to the facts in the indictment, and we believe that this evidence cannot be taken into consideration because it turned up in the course of the proceedings. I would like to say something in connection with the issue of persecution or aiding persecution, as mentioned by the Prosecutor in the indictment. I'm sorry. Just a moment. I lost my papers. The Prosecutor stated in the indictment that because of the actions committed by Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic of taking their families away from the area which was allegedly to be attacked and not informing the Muslims of the imminent attack, and of being present in uniforms and with weapons on that day, the Prosecutor alleges that they aided persecution. I believe that the legal standard applied by the Trial Chamber in the Tadic case as to whether a person can be responsible for participating in a crime perpetrated by others, that the same standard should be applied in this case also, that the intention to participate in the commission of a crime should be proved, that the perpetrator acted with this intention, and that his actions contributed significantly to the commission of the crime. This significant contribution is explained by the Trial Chamber, when it says that the commission of a crime would not have taken place in the same way had the accused not undertaken certain actions. Therefore, the presence of a person in the area where a crime was committed must be conscious and a causal connection must be established between the person's presence and the commission of the crime. In relation to the fact that he facilitated the commission of a crime by not informing his Muslim neighbours, this would have been aiding by omission, but for this kind of collaboration to be established, we must first see what the legal duty of the person is to do this. We have to see what his duties were in order to establish that he omitted to perform his duty, leading to legal consequences. I believe that the omission of a village guard does not have this weight, even if the Prosecutor was able to prove that the accused were aware of what was going to happen. As regards facilitating the commission of a crime by taking away one's family, I think this is absurd, because according to the principle that everyone has the right to protect himself and his family and is not duty-bound to put his life and his family's life at risk, even if the Prosecutor were to prove that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic had some knowledge or awareness of the act, all these acts would not have this weight, nor would they have such an effect that we could say that their contribution was essential and significant. Therefore, I propose that in relation to all the counts of the indictment, the Trial Chamber should find Mirjan Kupreskic not guilty, and I join my colleague, Mr. Radovic, in his proposal that he should be temporarily released from detention. They gave themselves up voluntarily, they have spent two years in The Hague at the trial, they have not caused any problems, there were no problems in the detention unit, and, on the other hand, we consider that the evidence offered by the Prosecutor does not indicate that these people are especially dangerous. Therefore, we consider that the Trial Chamber should, once again, reconsider its ruling and should release these people temporarily from detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we still have 15 minutes, before I call upon another Defence counsel to start -- I think it will be Counsel Krajina -- may I ask you a question, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Not in the oral argument, but in your written brief, you attach importance to alleged crimes, massacres, committed by Muslims against Croats in many villages before, during, or after the events we are discussing; namely, the 16th of April, 1993. What legal inference do you draw from those events, the alleged serious crimes committed by Muslims against Croats?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that the Prosecutor's introduction to this trial and the general picture he attempted to present at this trial is incorrect. First of all, I consider that the events which took place during 1993, in January, February, and March of 1993, do not indicate that the political and military objectives of the HVO were directed at eliminating Muslims from this area. I, in fact, consider the very opposite. All of 1993, as is evident from the testimonies of witnesses who testified here, was such that the Muslim army, on several occasions, initiated conflicts. The first conflict they initiated was when they set up a roadblock in Kacuni, which in fact led to the January conflict, and in that conflict, the Muslims won. They cleansed the whole area between Kacuni and Bilalovac, and on that occasion, over a hundred Croatian houses were destroyed. All of these villages were ethnically cleansed of Croats, and, in this way, the Kiseljak area was cut off from the area of the Lasva River Valley. So what we are saying is that the HVO was then on the defensive and was weaker than the Muslim side. The crimes, and we mentioned the crimes in Dusina, Nazerovici, Oseliste, were in fact crimes which took place because the Muslim army had this kind of orientation and was cleansing this area of Croats. So in my opinion, the basic tenets of the Prosecution that the Croatian army was on the offensive ever since the HVO was established, and what its aims were, are not correct. No witnesses have been brought forward to talk about the suffering of Muslims in these areas. We do not believe that one crime can be justified by another, but we are saying that the overall picture presented by the Prosecutor is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I assume Counsel Krajina would prefer to start when we resume after the coffee break, so that he can have an hour and a half. Let us now take a longer coffee break of, say, 15 minutes. So we will resume at 12.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. With the amended indictment confirmed on the 10th of March, 1998, the Prosecutor has charged Vlatko Kupreskic under point 1, crime against humanity, persecution on political, racial and religious grounds, punishable under 5(a) of the Statute; and counts 12 to 15 for two crimes against humanity, murder, and two counts of violations of customs of war recognised by Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions. After the evidence has been presented, we feel that the allegations from the indictment have not been proven, and the only proposition of the Defence is that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic should be acquitted of all counts he is charged with. This position is based on the following: With regard to Count 1, persecution, the accused Vlatko Kupreskic is accused of the following acts: Under 9 it is said that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic assisted in the preparation of the April attack on civilians in Ahmici and Santici by participating in military training and arming; by evacuating Bosnian Croats the night before the attack; by organising HVO soldiers; by organising arms and ammunition in and around the villages of Ahmici and Santici; prepared his home and the homes of his relatives as a starting position and a firing position for the attack; and concealed from other inhabitants that an attack was imminent. Also under point 1 it is stated that in the period from October '92 until April '93, Vlatko Kupreskic had persecuted Bosnian Muslim inhabitants of Ahmici, Santici, and surrounding, on political, racial or racial grounds; planning, organising and carrying out the attack intended to remove or cleanse all Bosnian Muslims from that village and the surrounding area; and that, in the context of that persecution, he participated, aided, or in other ways abetted the deliberate killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians, the comprehensive destruction of Bosnian Muslim homes and property, and the organised detention and expulsion of Bosnian Muslims from Ahmici, Santici and its environs. Bearing in mind the fact that the burden of proof is with the Prosecutor, let us review which of the allegations have been -- testimony has been provided for by the Prosecution and for which charges no evidence was tendered, even though charges have been made against Vlatko Kupreskic. Let us go one by one. The participation in military training, the Prosecution has not produced any evidence in support of this accusation. The evacuation of Bosnian Croat civilians in the night prior to the attack, no evidence presented by the Prosecution. Organising HVO soldiers, no evidence presented by the Prosecution. Organising weapons and ammunition in and around Ahmici and Santici, no evidence presented by the Prosecution. As for the background of the indictment, the Prosecutor with respect to Vlatko Kupreskic presented only indirect evidence meant to suggest that Vlatko Kupreskic had prepared his house as a location from which firing was made during the attack, and consequently kept secret from other residents of Ahmici that an attack was imminent. We shall return to these allegations later on. Furthermore, the incriminations from Count 1, that is, deliberate and systematic killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians, the Prosecutor presented evidence only with respect to counts 12 to 15, probably believing that if these counts would be proven, they would automatically prove the charges from Count 1. Since no evidence has been produced for this charge under Count 1, we shall discuss them in the course of the analysis of evidence presented for counts 12 to 15. Regarding the charge, comprehensive destruction of Bosnian Muslim homes and property, the Prosecutor has also not presented any evidence pertaining to the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. The organised detention and expulsion of Bosnian Muslims from Ahmici, Santici and its environs, again the Prosecutor presented no evidence pertaining to the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. Therefore, under Count 1 of the indictment, the accused Vlatko Kupreskic has been charged with numerous acts, the majority of which the Prosecution never even attempted to prove, as indeed no evidence could be found for such allegation, nor does it exist. The only thing the Prosecution attempted to prove is the following, starting from a fact that the Defence has not disputed, and that is that on the critical date of the 16th of April, '93, unknown soldiers were shooting in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house: The Prosecution has attempted by indirect evidence to say that Vlatko Kupreskic, knowing that the attack was imminent, lent his house to the soldiers as a firing position and thus participated in the persecution. For that purpose the Prosecution witnesses L, M, O, B, T and G have testified. What did these witnesses say? Witness L claims that on the 15th of April, 1993, he saw the accused Vlatko Kupreskic sitting with Ivica and Mirko Vidovic, having beer in front of his shop, and that at the same time there was some 10 soldiers in the warehouse of the shop; and that on the same day, while passing by the accused's house, he saw some 30 soldiers in black uniforms on the balcony of the house. Witness M claims that on the 15th of April, 1993, she saw four to five soldiers enter the basement or the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic. Witness O says that at around 3.45 on the 16th of April, 1993, he saw the light on in Vlatko Kupreskic's house. These witnesses, by this evidence, were to have confirmed the submission of the Prosecution that Vlatko Kupreskic was in cohort with the army and therefore gave his house to be used for military purposes. Who are these witnesses and what are their statements like? Witness L is a person without employment, with damaged mental health, prone to alcohol abuse. His health condition has been testified to by numerous residents of Ahmici in this Court, among whom are Ljuba Vidovic, Gordana Cuic and Ivica Kupreskic. In his testimony, Witness L states that immediately prior to the event that he testified about, he had had three glasses of brandy. He could not precisely define the time when he allegedly saw the accused, not even the date. In each of the previously made statements he gave a different time of the event and so on. The only point where he remained consistent was that at the critical time, he saw the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in the company of Ivica Kupreskic and Mirko Vidovic. Ivica Kupreskic and Mirko Vidovic have also testified in Court, and Vlatko Kupreskic himself testified about this event. Ivica Kupreskic stated that at that time he was with Vlatko Kupreskic, travelling from Split to Vitez. This was confirmed by Vlatko Kupreskic and numerous witnesses, including Ankica Kupreskic, Ljubica Kupreskic, Radoslav Simovic and (redacted). The appropriate travelling documents have been presented to the Court and we will be coming to them a little later. Mirko Vidovic, whom Witness L allegedly saw with the accused and the soldiers on the 15th of April, 1993, was at that time in Germany. During his testimony, Mirko Vidovic provided the Court with documents proving his stay in Germany: HVO permit for the trip to Germany, his passport, and the certificate of the city of Frankfurt. These were tendered Exhibits D28/3, D29/3 and D30/3. In his testimony of the 22nd of March, 1993, he confirmed that in the period from the 1st of April 1993 until June 1995 he was outside Bosnia-Herzegovina and Ahmici. Witnesses Gordana Cuic, Mirko Vidovic's sister, and Rudo Vidovic, Mirko Vidovic's brother, and witness Alojz Vidovic, confirmed that Mirko Vidovic could not possibly have been in Ahmici at the time he was allegedly seen by Witness L. Therefore, the testimony of Witness L, in our view, is absolutely unacceptable and unreliable, since it is in direct contradiction with the facts documented by the aforesaid witnesses, who claim that it was not possible for Witness L to see what he testified about. Bearing in mind the physical and mental condition of Witness L, and the fact that he had consumed alcohol just then, we feel that this testimony should be dismissed. Witnesses M and O are husband and wife, who, as refugees, were living with Witness L, and their testimony has no direct bearing with the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, but it was used to corroborate the testimony of Witness L, which obviously on its own cannot stand when contrasted against the Defence witnesses' testimonies and the documents presented. From the contents of the testimonies of Witnesses M and O, nothing can be found that would concretely point to the involvement of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in the preparations of the attack, as these witnesses did not even see him. But apparently the light was on for a moment in the house, and I don't know what kind of a conclusion can be derived from that of any significance. If we view testimonies of Witnesses M and O as separate evidence, they have no probative value, in our opinion, nor is there any logic in linking them with the testimony of Witness L, which is absolutely unacceptable. For the above reasons we feel that on the basis of the testimonies of Witnesses L, M, and O, the role of Vlatko Kupreskic cannot be proven regarding the accommodation of the army in Ahmici or in his house. A similar role regarding creating the impression of the involvement of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in the events prior to the 16th of April, 1993 was played by Witness B, who allegedly, on the 15th of April, passing by car in front of the Vitez Hotel in Vitez, looked for a moment, and at a distance of 30 metres saw the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in civilian clothes, standing some 10 metres away from the entrance into the hotel with three persons in uniform. The questions arising from this testimony is whether from that distance and the manner of the observation, from a moving car, it is possible to recognise a person. Expert witness Professor Wagenaar, who presented his expert testimony on the possibility of recognising persons at a distance, did not consider this recognition to be acceptable. Besides, Witness B had been living away from Ahmici for years, due to his work and service, and therefore had not been seeing Vlatko Kupreskic to be able to know well his outside appearance. Another objection to this testimony is that it is in contradiction with the testimonies of all previously mentioned witnesses who testified that the accused at that time was on his way from Split, as well as the documents presented with regard to that trip. It may perhaps be of interest that Witness B, at the time he was testifying about, was a security officer of the Bosnian army, who, by the nature of his work, had to collect all information about persons who were in any way involved in military and war activities against the Muslims. Even such a witness had no knowledge of the alleged activities of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, as mentioned in the indictment. Had there been any such activities, this witness would certainly have been among the first to be aware of it and to tell us about them. The next witness, Witness T, in his testimony says that in the autumn of 1992, during the Serb aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the evening, passing not far from the house of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, saw the accused and his wife, Ljubica, and another person, carrying what she thought were automatic weapons out of the car into the house. The very fact that this testimony relates to a period in time when the only ongoing conflict was the one with the Serbs, and when the Croats and Muslims were military and political allies, makes unacceptable bringing this evidence in connection with the alleged armament of units to fight the Muslims. The truthfulness of Witness T's statements has been rebutted entirely by the accused Vlatko Kupreskic and witness Ljubica Kupreskic. As the only possibility, they agree that Witness T may have seen them unloading some goods, as this is something they frequently did when they were storing those goods in their warehouse. The objective and possibility of identifying objects that were being unloaded from the car as weapons, bearing in mind the manner, the place and the time of observation, also excludes the reliability of this testimony. Finally, Prosecution Witness G, who claims that, six days after the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993, allegedly he saw the accused, from a distance of some 300 metres, enter with a group of people the house of Sakib Ahmic and carrying something out of the house. What was the purpose of this testimony, which is outside the time covered by the indictment, except perhaps to try to portray the image of the accused, who, allegedly, searches through abandoned houses for material gain? What is the credibility of a recognition from a distance of 300 metres by a witness who, six days previously, had experienced a terrible family tragedy, had been unconscious, without food and water, and was only 13 years of age at the time? Can such a testimony be accepted, when the witness claims, among other things, that he recognised the accused in a car, a blue Yugo 45, not knowing that Ivica Kupreskic had the same car as Vlatko Kupreskic? Your Honours, those were the Prosecution witnesses, on the basis of which attempts are being made to prove the involvement of Vlatko Kupreskic in planning and organising the expulsion of Muslims from Ahmici. How can such evidence be accepted, when not a single one of these witnesses specified an act by the accused which would, without any doubt, reflect criminal behaviour by the accused in line with the charges in Count 1? Not one of these Prosecution witnesses has claimed that the accused was involved in the persecution of Muslims from Ahmici. Not even the intelligence officer, Witness B, said that not on the fact that somebody was standing in front of the Vitez Hotel on the 15th of April can any convincing conclusion be drawn about the activities of that person. Combining such indirect evidence into a story about the involvement of the accused in planning and executing persecution we consider to be unacceptable, as there is simply not sufficient evidence to make such a story credible. If we also refer to Defence witnesses rebutting the Prosecutor's interpretation of the evidence, then the stories about the alleged role of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in the persecution of Muslims from Ahmici will be totally devoid of content. As for so-called material evidence relating to Count 1 of the indictment, in the course of the proceedings, the Prosecutor tendered documents marked P329 and P335. These documents were intended to shed light on the alleged connection between Vlatko Kupreskic and HVO structures and indicate that Vlatko Kupreskic was mobilised on the 16th of April, 1993 and that he was posted to the duty of deputy health officer. The first objection that can be made with respect to this evidence is that even if these documents were authentic, they cannot be taken into consideration for the charges, as even the indictment does not allege that HVO membership, and even as a deputy health commander, in itself means criminal responsibility, the more so as recruitment or mobilisation is a legal obligation that cannot be avoided without sanctions, and since participation in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, even serving in an enemy army, is an act that has been amnestied by all participants in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This has been confirmed by the testimony of the judge of the supreme court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this court. The second objection to these documents is that the information stated in them is not true. We can start with Prosecution evidence P329; namely, a certificate issued by the Vitez Regiment on the 4th of June, 1996 which establishes that Vlatko Kupreskic performed the duty of the deputy commander in charge of health in the period between the 16th of April, 1993 and the 15th of January, 1996. Under pseudonym DA/5, a witness testified with respect to whether the information from these certificates is true or not. She, at the critical time, worked in the recruitment and assignments department of the Vitez Regiment. This witness stated that she personally drafted Vlatko Kupreskic only in the summer of 1993, sometime in June or July, and posted him to the duty of organising the medical service. This witness has confirmed that she knew that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic was incapable of military service and that he had been exempt from military service due to a heart condition. This witness also confirmed the authenticity of Defence Exhibits D13/3, D14/3, D15/3, D16/3, and D17/3; that is to say, the military ID of the accused, the decision of the Medical Board of Appeal of 1993, the letter of discharge from the Military Academy Hospital, the decision of the Defence Administration from Travnik, and the certificate on his incapacity for military service, that is, of the accused, of 1998. All of these documents indubitably indicate that Vlatko Kupreskic, due to his heart condition, was declared incapable for military service before the war, during the war, and that he is recorded as such until the present day in the military files. For the purpose of evaluation and being exempt from military service, he was, during the war, sent to a medical board of the military which declared him exempt. It was true that he was later recruited into the medical service, the medical corps, which the accused himself confirmed during the course of his testimony, stating that it was in the month of September 1993, in a situation when this mobilisation was carried out forcibly. The manner and the time of the recruitment and mobilisation of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic was also confirmed by witness Zoran Drmic before this court. He was present when Vlatko Kupreskic was mobilised, as he was then working in the same office with Witness DA/5 on maintaining military records of persons liable for military obligation. The content of this testimony is identical to the claims made by Witness DA/5 and the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, as well as to those of the witness Ljubica Kupreskic, who also testified with respect to these circumstances. Witness DA/5 has also rebutted the accuracy of the information from Prosecution Exhibit P329, claiming that it was not possible for the accused to have been conscripted on the 16th of April, 1993, as she personally mobilised him much later; that is to say, on the 16th of April, 1993, the post of health deputy, stated in the aforesaid certificate, did not exist at all. The witness claims that it was not until June or July 1993 that the medical platoon was established. Witness DA/5 also explained that the certificate, Prosecution Exhibit P329, was issued upon the request of the person it pertains to, who could, based on such certificates of participation in war, be entitled to certain ownership rights, such as the right to hold shares of the BiH Federation. In order to make it possible for people to exercise these rights, to the greatest extent possible, the authorities used to write in the date of the 16th of April, 1993, when the war began, as the date when their participation in the war commenced. That is how this date made it into this certificate, P329. Witness DA/5 also commented on Prosecutor's Exhibit P353, the report on mobilisation, in which there is mention made of the name of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. The witness explained that this report only contains the following information; that is, that in the period between the 16th and 28th of April, 1993, mobilisation was carried out, but it does not show exactly when particular individuals were mobilised. Numerous other witnesses also pointed out the inaccuracies from this report, claiming that it simply represents a list of male persons who were to be mobilised. This evidence of the Prosecutor had one purpose only, and that is to show some kind of active role of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in the HVO and his alleged membership in the HVO from the 16th of April, 1993. We are of the opinion that dozens of witnesses have rebutted the accuracy of this and other documents on HVO membership, as it is common knowledge that in post-war Bosnia and Herzegovina, almost everyone could have the date of the 16th of April, 1993 recorded as the starting date of their participation in the BH war, all of it, of course, to enable them to exercise their right to hold BH Federation shares. Apart from that, Witness DA/5 and Zoran Drmic, the persons who personally and directly handled the conscription/mobilisation of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, indubitably rebutted in their testimonies the accuracy of the information contained in documents P329 and P335; that is, the allegation that Vlatko Kupreskic was mobilised on the 16th of April, 1993. It should also be pointed out that not a single witness who was examined in the course of these proceedings could state that he saw the accused Vlatko Kupreskic as a member of any military unit at that time, and not even having heard anyone else say so. This exhausts what we wish to say in connection with Prosecution evidence in respect of the responsibility of Vlatko Kupreskic for Count 1. We are of the opinion that not one of these pieces of evidence taken separately could stand an inaccuracy test with respect to the rebuttal evidence of the Defence. Furthermore, not one of these pieces of evidence contains sufficient elements for establishing any action of the accused that could be incriminated with respect to Count 1 of the indictment. Therefore, we are convinced that they have to be dismissed as irrelevant and lacking credibility. With respect to the claims of the Prosecution about the alleged involvement of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in the events described in Count 1 of the Prosecution, the Defence has offered evidence that endeavoured to provide a reconstruction of the life and behaviour of the accused in the period pertaining to the indictment and prove that accusations against Vlatko Kupreskic are unfounded, as he had no role in the events mentioned in the indictment. Elaborating further on that, the main points of the Defence with respect to Count 1 have been as follows: In the time prior to the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993, Vlatko Kupreskic did not have any military, political, or other prerogatives that could suggest that he could participate in preparing, planning, or carrying out the expulsion or persecution. At the time pertaining to the indictment, Vlatko Kupreskic was not even mobilised and did not take part in any military units, not even in the village guards. Throughout this period, he was exclusively involved in his commercial trade. Vlatko Kupreskic did not know, nor could have known, that a conflict could break out in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. Vlatko Kupreskic did not hand over his house to soldiers for combat engagement; it was taken over forcibly by soldiers, after he had abandoned it in order to go to a shelter, and then these soldiers took action from that house. Vlatko Kupreskic's attitude towards his Muslim neighbours was the same before, during, and after the war. We are going to present a brief reminder of the evidence presented by the Defence to corroborate these theses. Not one of the witnesses, neither of the Prosecution nor of the Defence -- and numerous witnesses were asked to testify with respect to these circumstances -- had ever said that they saw the accused Vlatko Kupreskic acting politically or militarily, that they ever saw him in uniform or carrying weapons. No one ever said that Vlatko Kupreskic had any kind of prerogatives or authority on the basis of which he might have had more information than any other resident of Ahmici, be him a Muslim or a Croat. Defence Exhibit D18/3, authorised by witness Rudo Kuvenja, states that Vlatko Kupreskic was not even a member of the HDZ, which was a political organisation which was, at that time, joined by almost all Croats. He was not a member of any other political organisation either. Not one of the witnesses stated that the outward behaviour of Vlatko Kupreskic provoked, in any way, national ethnic intolerance or hatred. On the contrary, all witnesses confirmed that in his job and behaviour, at work and in his personal conduct, he did not discriminate between Croats and Muslims, or people of any other ethnicity. Our second thesis is that Vlatko Kupreskic was not engaged in the military, and this has been proven by means of documents certifying his incapacity for military service; namely, D13, D14, D15, D16, D17, and the testimonies of Witness DA and Zoran Drmic, which we mentioned early, and the fact that no one ever saw him in uniform or carrying a weapon, not even in the village guards. That Vlatko Kupreskic at the time was exclusively involved in his own trade was mentioned by numerous witnesses of the Defence and the Prosecution, who testified with respect to those circumstances; notably, Vlado Alilovic, who at the time worked in the logistics department of Vitez that was in charge of issuing trade permits for businesses. This witness confirmed that the accused, throughout the period leading up to the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993, conducted his own commercial business. The same witness confirmed the authenticity of Defence Exhibits D10/3, D11/3; that is to say, the general permit for commercial trade and the permit for the movement of persons and goods, those being the documents related to the business of the accused in the period prior to the conflict. The Defence has maintained and continues to maintain that Vlatko Kupreskic could not have known that the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993 would break out. He could not have known because, from the early morning of the 14th of April, 1993 to the evening of the 15th of April, 1993, he was away on a business trip in Split, in the Republic of Croatia. Consequently, on the day when there could have been some preparations for the attack, he simply was not physically present in Ahmici, and therefore he could not have participated in any of it. Witnesses who were travelling with him were examined with respect to these circumstances; namely, Ivica Kupreskic; Ankica Kupreskic; a Muslim witness, pseudonym DE, who met him on the way; then Witness Radoslav Simovic, at whose house he spent the night between the 14th and 15th of April, 1993, in Baska Voda in Croatia; and a Muslim witness, DF, to whose place the accused was supposed to take part of the goods he brought from Split; and Vlatko's wife, Ljubica Kupreskic. The accused himself also testified with respect to these circumstances. Regarding this trip, appropriate official documents were presented that had to be obtained at the time for the purpose of travel, those being D24/3, that is, a travel warrant; D25/3, a permit for the trip of Ivica Kupreskic; D26/3, permit for the trip of Vlatko Kupreskic; D27/3, a road map marked by Ivica Kupreskic during the course of his testimony. So many pieces of evidence were presented with regard to this trip that the Defence considers it indisputable. So to summarise, Vlatko Kupreskic arrived in Ahmici only in the evening of the 15th of April, 1993, and saw nothing special going on in his house or in his shop that would suggest the events of the next day. On that day, on the 15th of April, 1993, Vlatko and Ivica Kupreskic brought Ivica's wife, Ankica, from Split to Ahmici. Until then Ankica had been in Germany as a refugee. It would have made no sense, Your Honours, that they should have brought her back on that very day had they known that there would be an armed conflict on the very next day, the very next morning. Vlatko's children went to school normally on that day, like all other children, Croat and Muslim, on the 15th of April, 1993. Vlatko's wife, Ljubica Kupreskic, took her driver's exam on that day, the 15th of April, 1993, which is corroborated by her testimony in this Court. How could it be claimed, in spite of all this evidence, that Vlatko Kupreskic knew that there was to be a conflict? His behaviour and his movement in the days prior to the conflict rebut this absolutely. And when indeed did Vlatko Kupreskic learn about the attack? He was the last one to know among his Croat neighbours. He was the last one to be informed by telephone, when everybody had already left their homes. This was clearly confirmed by the testimony of Ivica Kupreskic, Ljubica Kupreskic, and Vlatko Kupreskic himself, respectively. The Prosecution claims that Vlatko Kupreskic knew about the conflict and that he kept it secret from his Muslim neighbours. Rather, it could be said that if anything at all was known, it was kept secret from him, because he was the last to find out. He did not even evacuate his father from the house, as he did not know what would happen. Vlatko Kupreskic did not hand over his house to the soldiers as a firing point. The military did not ask anyone for permission to enter their house or any other building. Vlatko's house was in a position of tactical importance. The road between Upper and Lower Ahmici could be controlled from it, and any army would have taken it during combat action. And in that context, a house owner cannot refuse that at all. This was corroborated by an English officer, Colonel Watters, in his testimony before this Court as well. Vlatko Kupreskic left the house with his family before the soldiers arrived, and went to the shelter, not knowing at all that the military would come to his house. His father remained in the house and later related that the soldiers forcibly took the house, damaging the door, and then also searched the house afterwards. They plundered and took away Vlatko's property. Soldiers, who would have arranged their coming with the house owner beforehand, probably would not have behaved that way. This is what can be concluded on the basis of the testimony of Vlatko Kupreskic, of Ljubica Kupreskic, Defence Exhibit D12/3, on the damage done to the house, and the testimony of Vlado Alilovic. It is the fact that on the 16th of April, 1993, the soldiers took the house of Vlatko Kupreskic and engaged in combat from it, but Vlatko Kupreskic cannot be charged with it, for two reasons: First, because he did not know that soldiers would take his house and fire from it. And secondly, because the military cannot be prevented from doing so by anyone. Vlatko Kupreskic cannot be held responsible for what was done without his knowledge and which was not in his power to prevent. The Defence also wanted to show that Vlatko Kupreskic's attitude towards Muslims was the same before, during, and after the war. Before and during the war, not a single witness, either for the Prosecution or the Defence, said that there was any discrimination on religious, ethnic or political grounds in the behaviour of the accused. In the period after the war, in spite of the serious allegations because of which Vlatko Kupreskic is on trial before the International Tribunal today, he still has the same relationships with Muslims as before. His family continues to live in Ahmici, Muslims still come to his shop, and Muslims from Ahmici, witnesses too, and victims of the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993, still respond to the summons of this Court to testify about the way these events occurred. And as many as 12 Muslims from Ahmici have given their statements about the character of the accused. Had Vlatko Kupreskic done what is written -- what he is accused of in the indictment, these statements would not have been made, nor would these witnesses have appeared before the Court. Therefore, the Defence considers that with respect to Count 1, it has presented evidence which makes these allegations totally unacceptable with respect to the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. As for the legal positions with respect to the responsibility of the accused for persecution, in this case the Prosecutor advocates the thesis that in order to prove the penal responsibility of Vlatko Kupreskic, it is sufficient to show that he knew that the soldiers would use his house for the attack, and that he agreed to that, giving his support to it. We consider this premise to be purely theoretical, because the Prosecutor has not proved that the accused knew what would happen or shown that he acted in a way that showed that he consented to the consequences or wanted them. The position of the Defence with respect to the responsibility for persecution is identical to the position of the Supreme Court of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation, which seeks a direct intention as a form of consciousness which the accused has, an intention that can be clearly seen from concrete and individual actions of the accused. We refer to the verdict of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the Federation, and the judgement of the higher court in Sarajevo, which have been admitted as Defence Exhibits D31/3 and D32/3, and the testimony of the President of the Supreme Court of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation before this Court. By presenting this evidence of the legal practice in the Federation of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Defence wish to show that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, with evidence presented against him with respect to Count 1, with no concrete acts of commission, with not an established form of consciousness and of an act and its consequences, could not be sentenced before a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the country where the acts alleged in the indictment were committed, and the country whose citizen he is. It is therefore our position that Vlatko Kupreskic cannot be sentenced for Count 1 of the indictment, either in the Netherlands or any other country where international law is applicable. Your Honours, we would like to end our presentation as regards Count 1, and my colleague will now refer to Counts 12 to 15 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in Counts 12 to 15 of the indictment, Vlatko Kupreskic has been charged with having committed two criminal acts: A crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(a), murder, of the Statute of the Tribunal; and two criminal acts of violation of the laws and customs of war punishable under Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal, as recognised by Article 3(1)(a), cruel treatment of the Geneva Conventions. These allegations pertain to the events of the 16th of April, 1993, and according to the indictment of that day, there were soldiers in Vlatko Kupreskic's house who used the house as the starting point from where they shot at Bosnian Muslim civilians. The accused Vlatko Kupreskic has been charged with being together with HVO soldiers in front of the house when the Pezer family, together with other Bosnian Muslims, ran past his house, fleeing for their lives, and that Vlatko, together with the HVO soldiers from the position in front of his house, where they were aiding and abetting each other, participated in the wounding of Dzenana Pezer and one other woman, and the murder of Fata Pezer. This is what is alleged against Vlatko Kupreskic. The Defence is of the opinion that after the presentation of evidence, these allegations have not been proved and therefore proposes that Vlatko Kupreskic be acquitted of charges contained in Counts 12 to 15. We base this opinion on the evidence presented by the Defence, which has clearly shown the following: Vlatko Kupreskic was not present at the place where these events took place on the day in question. Secondly, the Pezer family and the group were attacked in a spot which cannot be seen from Vlatko Kupreskic's house, so they could not have been hit by bullets fired from that house. And thirdly, the testimony of Witness Q, on which the accusations against Vlatko Kupreskic are founded, and who is the only one who claims to have seen Vlatko Kupreskic on the day in question, is totally unacceptable because this is not a credible witness. These are the three lines of Defence presented before this Court. Let us remind ourselves of the evidence presented. With respect to the claim or, rather, with respect to what the Defence maintains, that Vlatko Kupreskic was not at the scene of crime, has been shown by the testimony of Jozo Vrebac, Alojz Vidovic, Ruza Grgic, Ljubica Kupreskic, Gordona Cuic, Ivo Vidovic, Ljuba Vidovic, and the accused Vlatko Kupreskic himself. All of these witnesses have confirmed beyond a doubt that they saw Vlatko Kupreskic in a shelter for people not fit for military service, in Jozo Vrebac's house, from 6 a.m. until 10 a.m., and that he did not leave that shelter even for a moment. In the final brief of the Prosecutor, the presence of Vlatko Kupreskic in that shelter has not been challenged, but, rather, how the witnesses knew that he was there until 10 a.m., when some of them did not have watches and so on. However, I believe that several witnesses, both for the Prosecution and the Defence, who talked about the way these events took place, confirmed that the shooting stopped, the gunfire stopped, at 10 a.m., and this is when Vlatko Kupreskic first left the shelter, as these witnesses say. The attack on the Pezer family took place and finished between 8.30 and 9.00 a.m. at a place which is two kilometres distance from this shelter. The witnesses who testified with respect to these circumstances were selected among the hundreds of people who were in the shelter on that day, and this was no accident. They were summoned because Witness I mentioned them as people he saw entering Jozo Vrebac's shelter on that day. This witness stated that between 7.00 and 8.00 he was observing from his house the Croats entering Jozo Vrebac's house, and all the persons he listed and who were able to come to this court were called by us to testify to the fact that Vlatko Kupreskic was in the shelter. We consider that it has been established beyond doubt that Vlatko Kupreskic was in the shelter at this time, which means he could not have participated in the attack on the Pezer family. This is the first line of the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic. The second line of Defence was to establish the direction in which the Pezer family was moving at the time they were attacked, and the spot where Fata Pezer was killed and Dzenana Pezer wounded. The Prosecution claims that this group was moving from their house or, rather, from the shelter, along a path towards the woods in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house, and that this is where they were attacked. This direction lies to the north of the wood and the hill separating Lower Ahmici from Upper Ahmici, and there are some points along that route which can be seen from Vlatko Kupreskic's house. On the contrary, the Defence has established that the Pezer family were moving from Ismail Pezer's house, along a path on the south side, and that they were attacked on a part of the path which is behind a hill, when viewed from the accused's house, and that this hill obstructs the view. The Prosecution examined Witnesses Q, P, R, S and T. These witnesses are all members of the same family and they are very closely related. Their testimonies are, in our opinion, contradictory and prejudiced. They are not identical as regards their route, the point at which they entered the wood, the configuration of the terrain along which they passed, the places where they were wounded, and everything else they said in their previous statements made to other organs. Why do we consider the statements of these witnesses to be prejudiced? For the simple reason that we believe they want to support the statement made by Witness Q. Witness Q is the only one who accused Vlatko Kupreskic of the murder of Fata Pezer, thus drawing his entire family into this case, not leaving it open to them to give any other kind of testimony; otherwise, he would be accused of giving false evidence. That is why they were not impartial before this Court. The Prosecutor brought along a family which testified, but they also summoned Witness II, who claimed to have found the wounded Pezers near the top of the hill, but this witness also says that they were on the south side of the hill, and this place could not be seen from Vlatko Kupreskic's house. He said it was near the top of the hill in an attempt to support the statement given by Witness Q, who said that he dragged Fata Pezer's body toward the south side, which was sheltered. Witness II was unable to confirm before this Court that there were any wounds or any -- there was nothing on Fata Pezer's clothing to indicate that she was dragged over this terrain, and this witness, when cross-examined, was unable to dispute the testimony of other witnesses who had also seen the place where Fata Pezer's body lay. Among these witnesses was his brother, Witness CG. They all said that the body was considerably lower down, not near the top of the hill, thus excluding the possibility that the body was dragged down. There would have been no reason to drag the corpse downhill when Fata Pezer was already dead. The Prosecution presented another piece of evidence in favour of the thesis that the event took place where the Prosecution claims, and that is a place that is visible from Vlatko Kupreskic's house. That evidence is the allegation of Witness Q; we have that witness again, who, six years after the event, allegedly found some personal belongings of his near the top of the hill and claims that they were things that belonged to members of his family. The Defence considers this evidence totally unacceptable for a number of reasons. In the first place, not one of those objects 24 can be said, without any doubt, to belong to the (redacted) family. By their nature, those objects could belong to anyone or everyone. Furthermore, the traces of damage on those objects vary so much that it is clear that all those objects had not been in one place together throughout that time; namely, some things were charred, some were damaged, some were undamaged, and this cannot be the case if they were in the same bag, as claimed by Witness Q; not to say that even some objects had parts missing, and where were those parts if those objects were in one place all the time, et cetera? The area where these things are found is a wood, exposed to the climate, felling of trees, refugees passing by. All this shows that we cannot, under any circumstances, accept the allegation that those things had not been moved, that they were in one spot, and that they all belonged to the (redacted) family. Such evidence can be very seriously criticised, ranging from the way in which they were found onwards. So we are sure that this Court will reject this evidence as not credible. Therefore, on the basis of biased and contradictory statements by members of one and the same family, who experienced a very great personal tragedy on the 16th of April, which makes them less objective and absolutely negatively disposed towards their Croat neighbours, and the absolutely unacceptable evidence of the objects found, these were used by the Prosecution to prove the movement of the (redacted) family and the way in which they were wounded or killed. Contrary to this, the Defence, for these same events, produced the following evidence: We examined witnesses who, on the critical occasion, were in same group with the Pezer family, one of whom was wounded as a victim of the same act as Dzenana Pezer and Fata Pezer. We examined an eyewitness of the attack on the Pezer family. We examined witnesses who saw where the body of Fata Pezer lay. We presented expert witnesses in ballistics, forensic medicine, and geometry. On the basis of this evidence, the Defence believes that the direction of the movement stated by the Prosecution has been rebutted and that it has been proven that the Pezer family, from the time the attack started, was moving along the southern slope of the wood and could not have been directly hit from the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's house. Let us briefly review the evidence presented by the Defence. On the critical occasion, in the same group with the Pezer family were a number of other persons, including Court Witnesses CF and CE. These are witnesses of Muslim nationality who do not personally know Vlatko Kupreskic, and on the 16th of April, 1993, they were running for their lives in the same way as the Pezer family, moving with them in the same group. Witness CF, the witness we heard here, was wounded in the same shooting, at the same moment as Dzenana and Fata Pezer, and almost on the same spot, at a distance of only a few metres. Testifying in court and with a videotape, he described in detail the way and direction of movement of the group, where and how he was wounded, where and how Dzenana was wounded, and where and how Fata Pezer was killed. In his testimony, he said that the group was going along the lower side of the wood, on the southern side -- that is not visible from Vlatko Kupreskic's house -- that they were wounded with explosive ammunition that ricocheted from the trees and the forest. He saw the place where Dzenana Pezer was wounded and where Fata Pezer lay, and he has shown that place on the ground. He was a Court witness. Court Witness CE, a Muslim, the wife of Witness CF, who was moving with their son in the same group, described, in the same way as Witness CF, the direction of movement and the place of attack, confirming in its entirety the videotape on which CF indicates the critical spots. Therefore, two immediate eyewitnesses, victims who are absolutely impartial, who do not know the accused, Muslims, CF, who was himself wounded, claim something quite to the opposite than the Prosecution witnesses regarding the direction of movement and the way of wounding. They have no reason to help the accused, nor do they have any reason to support the testimony of Witness Q. They were free to testify the truth, and the Defence considers their testimonies to be absolutely credible and irrefutable. So those were actual participants and victims of the attack. Witness CG was also heard as an eyewitness because he was observing the event from in front of his position. He was attracted by their screams and calls for help when they were wounded. Where did CG see the event taking place? Exactly where Witnesses CF and CE said that the attack had occurred. Witness CG showed on the videotape from where he was watching and where he saw the wounding of the Pezers. This is a position from which Vlatko Kupreskic's house cannot be seen, as it is behind the hill. Witness CG is a Muslim from Ahmici, and we consider his testimony to be of special relevance. Three witnesses were heard in connection with the discovery of Fata Pezer's body on the day of the event and later. Those witnesses marked the position where they saw the body. The first of those witnesses was Prosecution Witness F. This Prosecution witness, in his testimony, said that on the 16th of April, 1993, he himself had suffered a grave tragedy and that, as he was passing through the woods, he came across the body of Fata Pezer. Where was the body? It was on the southern side of the wood, roughly near the place marked as the place of the killing of Fata Pezer by Court Witness CF. From that position, Vlatko Kupreskic's house cannot be seen. Here again, we have a Muslim witness who was a victim and a Prosecution witness, who certainly has no reason to support the Defence by pointing to the place where the body of Fata Pezer lay. Court Witness CH, a Muslim and a victim, who, together with a group of 10 to 15 other civilians from Ahmici, on that same day, several hours after the killing of Fata Pezer, passed along the southern side of the hill and the wood, along the path that goes from the Pezer houses to the shelter in Upper Ahmici, and who saw, along the path, the body of Fata Pezer. Where did she see the body? Roughly in the same spot as Witness F and Court Witnesses CF and CG. The testimony of this witness and the place she indicated on the videotape can be checked through the testimony of 10 to 15 people who were moving along with her, and we consider this testimony to be irrefutable. Witness Stipan Vidovic, a Croat from Ahmici, some ten days after the event, heard that there was a body in the wood, and he went to see who it was and to do something about it. He came across the body of Fata Pezer, notified the Red Cross, who then removed the body. Where did Stipan Vidovic find the body? On roughly the same place as the witnesses that we have mentioned so far. On the videotape, he showed that place in the wood. Therefore, a number of independent witnesses, including Prosecution witnesses, describing the different experiences, are unanimous in indicating the place where they saw the body of Fata Pezer. The place where they saw the body corresponds to the place marked by Court Witness CF as the place where he was wounded, where Dzenana Pezer was wounded, and where Fata Pezer was killed. The differences are a couple of metres, but it is always on the southern slope of the hill that is not visible from Vlatko Kupreskic's house. Not only does the position of the body exclude the possibility of direct hits from the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's house, but it absolutely eliminates the possibility that the body could have been dragged to that place from the top of the hill. Because of the inaccessibility of the terrain, the steep slope, the bumpy terrain, the thicket, the wood, all this makes it impossible to move a body, or to carry it, without visible injuries being made on the body. Something else that excludes the possibility of the body having been dragged from the top of the hill to the position where the witnesses saw the body: It makes absolutely no sense that anyone who is in mortal danger from the ongoing attack should drag a body of another person from one place to another on a difficult terrain, at some distance, after having established that the person is already dead and beyond help, and has next to him a wounded daughter who needs help. To act in this way would be quite illogical. The Defence took pains to establish the position of the body to prove their submission that the body remained at the place where they were attacked -- that is, that it wasn't moved -- and also to prove the path taken by the Pezers and the impossibility of them being attacked in the way claimed by the Prosecution. To compare the testimonies of all these witnesses who spoke about the position of the body, and to see whether they were talking about the same spot, we had expert testimony. On the basis of the testimony of the witness, this expert established the places on the ground and established that there is no optical visibility from any of those spots towards Vlatko Kupreskic's house, that all those places are at the same level, and that the distance between them is only a couple of metres. Expert witnesses Josip Skavic and Damir Catipovic performed a combined ballistic and forensic expertise in order to establish the mechanism and means with which Dzenana Pezer and Witness CF were wounded and where Fata Pezer were killed. What does these expert witnesses establish? They establish that the injuries of Dzenana Pezer and Witness CF could not have been inflicted in the way claimed by the indictment and Witness Q, because Dzenana Pezer's injury was inflicted on her right side and Witness CF's from above and from the front, none of which fits into the thesis of the possibility of a direct hit from the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's house at the column that had their backs turned to it and a hill on their right. Contrary to this, the findings of these two experts fully corroborate the mechanism of the wounding and the means of wounding as described in his testimony by Court Witness CF, and they eliminate the possibility of the column having been injured in the way described by Prosecution witnesses. When we review all the evidence that the Defence presented to prove the direction of movement of the Pezer group and the place of wounding and the killing of group members, we are of the opinion that there can be no doubt regarding what has been established, because all this evidence complements one another, although they were provided by a number of totally independent witnesses and experts. We consider the place of wounding to have been established in the lower section of the hill, on the southern side from where Vlatko Kupreskic's house cannot be seen, and where no one can be hit with direct shots coming from the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's house. Through the evidence reviewed so far, it is our submission that the Defence has proven two things: First, that Vlatko Kupreskic was not at the scene of the crime at the critical time; and second, that the Pezers could not have been wounded by shots fired from his house. Nevertheless, the Defence has devoted special attention to checking the credibility of Witness Q's statement and, in that respect, the statements of the other members of his family who appeared as Prosecution witnesses. The testimony of Witness Q is particularly interesting, as this witness was the only one of all the witnesses examined in these proceedings to have alleged that the accused, Vlatko Kupreskic, participated in the events of the 16th of April 1993, and that he himself saw him standing with a group of soldiers, shooting at Fata Pezer and the others. The entire indictment against Vlatko Kupreskic is based on this testimony for counts 12 to 15 and, in the opinion of the Defence, also for Count 1, because the indictment has been drafted in such a way that should the counts 12 to 15 be proven, they automatically prove Count 1 as well. So let us see exactly what Witness Q said. He said that he turned around for a moment and saw, at a distance of about 50 to 60 metres, the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in that particular group. The Prosecution investigator, Mr. Tucker, afterwards measured the distance and found it to be 53 metres. If we consider Witness Q's testimony, we can see that at the same time, the same place, the members of his family were there too, namely, Witnesses R, S, P, and T. Did any of them see Vlatko Kupreskic? No one did. Were they looking in the same direction as Witness Q did? Almost all of them looked the same way, but nobody saw Vlatko Kupreskic. Did Q tell any of them or anyone at all on that day or later that he saw Vlatko killing members of his family? No, he did not. Except to the Bosnian police and the Court. Dozens of witnesses were heard, Prosecution witnesses, who were in the immediate vicinity of Vlatko Kupreskic's house almost throughout the day of the 16th of April. They were either hiding with the intention of running away further later, or whatever. Practically all the persons who were in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house, they saw soldiers, they saw civilians. They identified Franjo Kupreskic as a civilian. They saw soldiers whom they could not recognise. One witness mentioned the names that they used -- that they called out to one another. How come no one ever saw Vlatko Kupreskic there? How is it possible that only Witness Q saw him? How come that his brother, Witness S, who on the same occasion stood together with him, turned around in the same direction, looked in that direction and heard later from him that it was Vlatko? How come that Witness S did not believe him? How come that he did not confirm what his brother had said?
